after.text:
Retire the issue: the ruling on stack-lifecycle-delegates-to-project-tooling removes the `stack` key from `.ok-planner/config.json`, so `stack.tag_variable` no longer exists and cannot collide with a declared port name. The sprint that carries that ruling removes the collision defect with the key, in [plumbline:stackDefects](plugins/ok/families/ok-planner/scripts/plumbline#L297-L324) and [stack:stack_defects](plugins/ok/families/ok-planner/scripts/stack#L288-L321), and true-up's config offer then names no key for it.

Rationale: the question of which name yields exists only while the stack tool sets a project-named variable to the run tag. Once the `stack` key retires, `ports` stays only as a setting the port registry reads, and no other config name competes with a port name.

before.text:
Keep the collision a stack defect: the owner repairs it by choosing another run-tag variable, and true-up's config offer refuses a port rename for it. Record in the corpus, beside the rule that binds host ports to declared port names, that the run-tag variable may not be a declared port name and that the variable is what yields.

Rationale: the config offer edits only the project's configuration, and the run-tag variable and the start command that reads it both live in one key there, so the offer can make the whole repair without touching a file the owner wrote elsewhere. A port rename (B) leaves every compose file and command that reads the port on the old name, which the compose port check then flags, so the offer would hand the owner the work the true-up story says an upgrade never costs. Accepting both keys (C) adds a special case to a rule that now has none, for a repair whose cheaper side is known. The flip case: if projects' compose files commonly read the run-tag variable too, such as for image tags, a variable rename reaches as many files as a port rename, and only the owner knows which is cheaper, so both keys (C) earns its special case.

messages.text: Recommendation now explains the retirement the ruling chose.

options.label: A
options.text: The collision is a stack defect (the code now): the corpus says the owner repairs it by choosing another run-tag variable, and true-up's config offer refuses a port rename. Cost: an owner who would rather rename the port edits the config by hand.

options.label: B
options.text: The collision is a ports defect: the defect text opens with `ports` again, the owner repairs it by renaming the port, and the offer refuses a run-tag variable change. Cost: the rename reaches every compose file and command that reads the port variable, which the offer cannot edit.

options.label: C
options.text: The collision belongs to both keys: true-up's config offer accepts a draft that changes either the run-tag variable or the port name. Cost: the one defect whose offer names two keys, a special case beside the rule that a defect's first word names its key.

problem:
When `.ok-planner/config.json` declares a port name that is also `stack.tag_variable`, the variable the stack tool sets to the run tag, true-up's config offer accepts only a draft that changes the `stack` key and refuses a draft that renames the port. No corpus artifact says which of the two names the owner repairs, and [story:true-up-project-estate](.ok-planner/design/stories/true-up-project-estate.md) owes the owner that upgrading the suite never costs them work they wrote.

The mechanism: `plumbline config-check` and `stack up` print the same defect, 'stack.tag_variable "<NAME>" is also a name ports declares, and the stack tool sets it to the run tag', from [plumbline:stackDefects](plugins/ok/families/ok-planner/scripts/plumbline#L297-L324) and [stack:stack_defects](plugins/ok/families/ok-planner/scripts/stack#L288-L321). True-up's [true-up:config_named_keys](plugins/ok/families/ok-planner/admin/true-up#L2778-L2779) names each config key whose name opens a defect's text, and [true-up:changed_keys](plugins/ok/families/ok-planner/admin/true-up#L2782-L2793) refuses a draft that changes any key not named, as [`admin/ADMINISTRATION.md`](plugins/ok/families/ok-planner/admin/ADMINISTRATION.md#L122) says of the `config` offer. So the first word of the defect text alone picks the key the owner may change: the text opens with `stack`, and a port rename is refused as 'ports (changed)'. The offer edits `.ok-planner/config.json` alone. The `stack` key holds the start command that reads the run-tag variable, so a draft can rename the variable and the start command's use of it in one key. A port name is read by the project's compose files and commands, which the offer does not touch, so a port rename inside the config alone leaves them reading the old name.

The state of play: before sprint certification of `2026-10-14-stack-lifecycle` (run converge-2026-10-15T011914), the text opened with 'ports', so the offer accepted only a port rename. The run's defect i16 re-worded it to open with `stack` and recorded the choice as question call i29, reasoning that a port rename reaches every compose file and command that reads the port variable, while the start command reads the run-tag variable. [decision:stack-ports-checked-as-a-suite-rule](.ok-planner/design/decisions/stack-ports-checked-as-a-suite-rule.md) binds each published host port to a declared port name and says nothing of the run-tag variable.

The ruling decides which name true-up's config offer lets the owner change when the two collide.

The sprint that carries that ruling removes the collision defect with the key, in [plumbline:stackDefects](plugins/ok/families/ok-planner/scripts/plumbline#L297-L324) and [stack:stack_defects](plugins/ok/families/ok-planner/scripts/stack#L288-L321), and true-up's config offer then names no key for it.

Rationale: the question of which name yields exists only while the stack tool sets a project-named variable to the run tag. Once the `stack` key retires, `ports` stays only as a setting the port registry reads, and no other config name competes with a port name.

messages.text: Prevent import cycles, and leave where shared code lives to each project. Step 2 of the reuse rule checks that an import does not close a cycle, as well as what the import weighs. Where reuse would close a cycle, the agent breaks the cycle so every import points one way, in whatever shape the project's own organization calls for. An import placed inside a function to dodge a circular-import error is a defect, fixed by breaking the cycle. A project checks for cycles with a tool for its language.

options.label: A
options.text: Prose rules only: step 2 weighs an import's direction, shared code moves down to the lowest package both callers may import, and a function-local import placed to dodge a cycle is a defect fixed by moving the code. Cost: a written constraint with no check, against the cheatsheet's rule that every constraint has one.

options.label: B
options.text: Prose rules plus a suite lint check: the project declares its layer order in ok-planner's configuration, and a new check in the suite's lint fails an import against it. Cost: per-language import parsing in a lint that today reads comments and compose files, a new configuration key with its config check and true-up offer, and an amendment to [decision:project-chooses-its-lint-checks](.ok-planner/design/decisions/project-chooses-its-lint-checks.md).

options.label: C
options.text: Prose rules plus a project-checked layering rule, after the stack-ports precedent: the suite states the rules, and a project with more than one package declares its layer order and checks it with an import linter for its language. Cost: a project that wires no such linter gets the text alone, and the suite cannot check the wiring.

options.label: D
options.text: Leave layering to each project's subjects and practices. Cost: the reuse rule keeps sending agents across package boundaries until an owner writes a practice, and every project words the rule its own way.

problem:
Plumbline's reuse rule tells an agent to import an existing function from wherever it sits, and no Plumbline rule says where shared code lives or which way an import may point. In a project with several packages, agents who follow the rule build import cycles between packages, so no package can be maintained on its own. The cheatsheet commits the suite to "Strict DRY: semantically identical logic lives in ONE place" and to "Every written constraint needs a check that fails on violation: layering → dependency lint", but no rule tells a project to declare its layers, so no project has a layering to lint.

The mechanism: section 6 of [plumbline-coding.md](plugins/ok/families/ok-planner/docs/plumbline-coding.md#L66-L72), "Import, never copy", says in step 1 "Where it exists, import it", and in step 2 "Where a dependency-split rule seems to block the import, read what the module actually imports before assuming." Step 1 sends the agent to the function's current home. Step 2 weighs how heavy an import is and never which way it points. Each reuse can add an edge up or across the package graph, and nothing mechanical refuses a cycle: the suite's lint runs five checks, comment hygiene, citation resolution, no tests, compose ports, and compose labels ([plumbline:LINT_CHECK_NAMES](plugins/ok/families/ok-planner/scripts/plumbline#L187)), and none reads imports. Where Python refuses a circular import at load time, an agent moves the import inside a function to get past the error instead of moving the shared code down.

The owner reports the harm from the LineScout platform (package `gridiq`), which runs Ruff and declares no layers: one import cycle of 12 units spanning its main services, three two-unit cycles, 13 imports of the project's own modules placed inside functions, two of them on the big cycle to dodge circular-import errors, and 12 of the 79 root modules, which act as the shared base, importing service packages. Each import was reasonable inside its task; together they keep the owner from splitting the platform into independently maintained parts. That evidence lies outside this tree.

The owner asks for rules that cover at least: the project declares its layer order and a lint fails an import that breaks it; before importing from a sibling or higher package, the agent moves the code down to the lowest package both callers may import; an import placed inside a function to dodge a circular-import error is a defect fixed by moving the code; and step 2 weighs an import's direction, not only its weight. The canonical rule files and the lint are this project's shipped product, so the change is the project's own, and the copies under `.claude/rules/` follow on the next `/ok`. Every line added to the rules costs context in every session, since [concept:cheatsheet](.ok-planner/design/concepts/cheatsheet.md) keeps that layer small. [decision:stack-ports-checked-as-a-suite-rule](.ok-planner/design/decisions/stack-ports-checked-as-a-suite-rule.md) is the precedent for a suite rule a project checks with the suite's lint where it applies, with a project lint, or with both. No corpus artifact speaks to import direction or layering.

The ruling decides what the suite prescribes about where shared code lives and how a project checks import direction.

recommendation.text:
State the layering rules in the suite and have each project check them with its own import linter. Step 2 of the reuse rule weighs an import's direction as well as its weight. Shared code lives in the lowest package every caller may import, and an agent moves a function down before importing it from a sibling or higher package. An import placed inside a function to dodge a circular-import error is a defect, fixed by moving the code. A project with more than one package declares its layer order and checks it with an import linter for its language. Record the rule as a suite decision beside the one for stack ports.

Rationale: this follows the stack-ports precedent, where the suite states a rule that holds for every project and lets a project check it with a lint that reads its own formats, which import graphs are: every language parses imports its own way, and mature import linters already exist for the common ones. It gives the cheatsheet's "layering → dependency lint" a layering to check, which prose alone (A) does not, and it costs a few lines of rules text where a suite check (B) costs a per-language import parser, a configuration key, and an offer. Leaving it to practices (D) leaves in place the rule that sends agents across packages, which is the harm reported. The flip case: if owners commonly run multi-package projects with no import linter wired, the rule stays text there, and a suite check (B) earns its parser, starting with the languages the suite's own users ship.

ruling.text: Prevent import cycles, and leave where shared code lives to each project. Step 2 of the reuse rule checks that an import does not close a cycle, as well as what the import weighs. Where reuse would close a cycle, the agent breaks the cycle so every import points one way, in whatever shape the project's own organization calls for. An import placed inside a function to dodge a circular-import error is a defect, fixed by breaking the cycle. A project checks for cycles with a tool for its language.

title: Plumbline says to import shared code but never where it lives, so agents build import cycles

messages.text: The ruling on stack-lifecycle-delegates-to-project-tooling replaces the mandated stack tool with optional helpers. Removal of a run's docker objects moves to the new docker sweep helper, which the reference .ok-planner/bin/stack calls. Revise this issue so its question, what evidence lets the tool conclude a run made no docker object when the daemon does not answer, targets the docker sweep helper.

after.label: A
after.text: The sweep reads silence as nothing made: where the daemon does not answer, the sweep removes nothing, reports that the daemon did not answer, and exits zero. Cost: a run that made labelled objects and lost its daemon before teardown ends with nothing that records those objects, in the reference tool and in every project's own teardown alike.

after.label: B
after.text: The sweep reports silence, and its caller decides: where the daemon does not answer, the sweep removes nothing and exits with a status of its own, distinct from success and from a refused removal. The reference stack tool records every daemon answer it observes, before and after its start command, on a failed start as on a passing one, and treats that status as done only for a run that recorded no answer. Cost: every project teardown that calls the sweep handles one more exit status, and a daemon started and stopped inside the start command, or started by a later verification step, still escapes the reference tool.

after.label: C
after.text: The sweep takes the evidence as an argument: the caller tells the sweep whether the run ever reached docker, and the sweep reads silence as nothing made only where the caller says the run did not. Cost: the evidence each project's tooling must collect, such as a probe around its own start, becomes part of the helper's interface, so the sweep no longer stands alone.

after.label: D
after.text: Silence leaves a docker-pending record: the sweep reports silence as in B, and the reference stack tool releases the run's ports and deletes its folder but keeps its entry marked as owing a docker sweep, which a later cleanup runs once the daemon answers. Cost: on a machine where docker is installed and never started, a pending entry stays for every run and the registry listing grows without bound.

before.label: A
before.text: The start-time answer decides (the code now): the corpus says a run whose daemon answered neither before its start command nor at `down` made no docker object. Cost: a start command that starts and later loses the daemon leaves labelled objects with no record.

before.label: B
before.text: Any answer the tool observes decides: the stack tool also probes the daemon after the start command exits, whether the start passed or failed, and `down` skips docker only where none of its probes answered. Cost: one more docker call on every `stack up`, and a daemon started and stopped inside the start command, or started by a later verification step, still escapes.

before.label: C
before.text: The answer at `down` alone decides: `down` skips docker whenever the daemon does not answer, and deletes the entry. Cost: a run known to have made labelled objects loses its entry while the daemon is stopped, and nothing later removes those objects.

before.label: D
before.text: An unreachable daemon leaves a docker-pending entry: `down` stops the process group, deletes the folder, and releases the ports, but keeps the entry marked as owing a docker removal, which a later cleanup performs once the daemon answers. Cost: on a machine where docker is installed and never started, a pending entry stays for every run and the registry listing grows without bound.

problem.after:
The ruling on stack-lifecycle-delegates-to-project-tooling replaces the mandated stack tool with optional helpers. One of them is a docker sweep that removes every docker object carrying a run's label or whose compose project equals the run's tag, and the reference `.ok-planner/bin/stack` calls it at `down` and in its cleanup. The sweep finds those objects by asking docker's daemon. Where the daemon does not answer, the sweep cannot list them, so it cannot tell a run that made no docker object from a run whose objects stay on disk while the daemon is stopped. No corpus artifact says what the sweep reports then, or what lets its caller treat the run as taken down. [story:verification-leaves-no-artifacts-behind](.ok-planner/design/stories/verification-leaves-no-artifacts-behind.md) owes the owner a way to have each run's artifacts removed once the run is over, and [decision:run-artifacts-recorded-by-the-stack-tool](.ok-planner/design/decisions/run-artifacts-recorded-by-the-stack-tool.md) says `down` removes every container, image, volume, and network that carries the label.

The mechanism the sweep inherits: [stack:start_run](plugins/ok/families/ok-planner/scripts/stack#L723) probes the daemon once with `docker version`, before it runs the start command, through [stack:docker_reached](plugins/ok/families/ok-planner/scripts/stack#L581-L589), and records the answer on the run's registry entry. At `down`, [stack:removal_steps](plugins/ok/families/ok-planner/scripts/stack#L638-L653) asks [stack:docker_out_of_reach](plugins/ok/families/ok-planner/scripts/stack#L592-L593) whether the recorded answer was no and a fresh probe also fails; where both hold, it skips every docker removal, and `down` deletes the entry. The cleanup's [stack:in_use](plugins/ok/families/ok-planner/scripts/stack#L816-L837) skips its running-container check on the same test. Where the start-time probe answered, `down` tries every docker removal, and a refused removal keeps the entry for a later cleanup, as [decision:run-artifacts-removed-with-the-run](.ok-planner/design/decisions/run-artifacts-removed-with-the-run.md) requires. The start-time answer lives on the reference tool's registry entry. A sweep usable alone, called from a project's own teardown, takes a tag and holds no such record.

The state of play: sprint certification of `2026-10-14-stack-lifecycle` (run converge-2026-10-15T011914) added the skip as defect i17. Before it, a run that made no docker object, taken down on a machine with Docker Desktop installed and stopped, kept its entry and its leased ports behind four docker refusals, and every later cleanup refused it again. The skip fixes that machine. Its gap is a run whose daemon came up after the start-time probe: a later stopped daemon reads as proof that the run made nothing. Under the helpers the question splits in two: what the sweep reports when the daemon does not answer, and which caller holds the evidence that a run never reached docker.

The ruling decides what evidence lets the docker sweep, or the caller that runs it, conclude that a run made no docker object when the daemon does not answer.
problem.before:

problem:
True-up never counts a file as a caller of a retired suite script where the file sits below any folder in the project that holds both `admin/true-up` and `admin/ADMINISTRATION.md`, so it removes the retired copy even where such a file still calls it. The mechanism: true-up finds callers of a retired script with `git grep -F` over the tracked files, repoints what it can, files an intake issue for each file it cannot repoint, and keeps the retired copy while such an issue names it. A path the running payload also carries is that proof, and it survives the working tree moving past the installed release, which the content match the fixer rejected does not. Its one false positive is a payload file newer than the installed release, which costs a kept copy and an issue until the next release: the cost the decision already accepts. messages.text:
Keep `.ok-planner/bin/stack` as the one required tool for drives and tests, and cut the friction for projects with their own stack tooling:

1. `stack down` also removes every docker object whose compose project equals the run tag. Coding rule 10 asks that each docker object a run makes be removed, by that compose project, by the run label, or by the stop command, and no longer requires the label. The lint retires its `compose-labels` check.
2. A new optional key, `stack.prepare`, names a command `stack up` runs under a lock before the start command, for setup many runs share. Its output outlives the run, `down` and `cleanup` leave it alone, and the project prunes it. A shared image or folder is named after its inputs, never `:latest`. A failed prepare opens no run.
3. `stack up` treats a port as taken when it fails to bind over UDP as well as TCP, and when a docker container on the host publishes it.
4. The stack tool serves drives and tests only. It mints no tag for release images, and a project's release scripts use a tag source of their own.

Replace the mandated stack tool with optional helpers, and return the process to v25.3.0's model, where each project runs its own stack commands.

1. The process prompts run the project's own commands. `/converge`'s drive and `/audit`'s deployments run the commands that the "Drive commands" section of `.ok-planner/review/project.md` names, as in v25.3.0. No prompt names a suite helper.
2. Remove the mandates: coding rule 10, the cheatsheet's "Per-run artifacts and verification stacks" section, the lint's `compose-ports` and `compose-labels` checks, and the `stack` key in `.ok-planner/config.json`. `ports` and `port_range` stay only as settings the port registry reads.
3. Ship helpers that a project may call from its own commands, each usable alone:
   - a tag generator at `.ok-planner/bin/run-tag`, with the same path and output as v25.3.0;
   - a port registry that leases and releases ports per tag, treats a port as taken when it fails to bind over TCP or UDP or when a docker container publishes it, and lists stale leases;
   - a docker sweep that removes every object carrying a run's label or whose compose project equals the run's tag;
   - a process-group helper that starts a command in a group of its own and later stops the group.

   `.ok-planner/bin/stack` stays as a reference start and stop built from the helpers, for a project with no stack tooling of its own.
4. Describe the helpers in a reference document outside the always-loaded rules, with the tag and port advice from v25.3.0's cheatsheet.
5. Each project's own tooling owes the stories `concurrent-stacks-without-port-collisions` and `verification-leaves-no-artifacts-behind`, and `/audit` checks them there.
6. True-up moves a v26.0.0 project's `stack` declaration back into its "Drive commands" section.

The suite fixes both the stack lifecycle and its one implementation: [decision:stack-tool-runs-each-run](.ok-planner/design/decisions/stack-tool-runs-each-run.md) makes [`.ok-planner/bin/stack`](.ok-planner/bin/stack) "the only way to mint a run tag", and [decision:ports-leased-from-a-project-range](.ok-planner/design/decisions/ports-leased-from-a-project-range.md) makes it the only source of a run's host ports, so a project that already runs isolated stacks with its own tooling must replace that tooling or conflict with it. The owner asks that the suite define the process and the verbs it requires, and let a project's configuration name the project's own implementation of each verb.

Observed in the GridIQ platform project (linescout/platform) on its `/ok` true-up from v25.3.0 to v26.0.0, which the owner then backed out:

- The project runs named stacks: `GRIDIQ_STACK=<name> bin/up` gives each stack a compose project name and a port block, which `src/gridiq/cli/instance.py` allocates and records in `.local/stacks/<name>.env`. `bin/dev`, `bin/down`, and `bin/device` read the same file. Drives use the stack `drive`, and build tasks start stacks of their own, such as `machines` and `outage`. It also runs project folders with recorded port blocks, per-stack device images, and its own cleanup verbs (`driver stop-unit-stacks`, `driver superseded-images`).
- The `port-range` offer would make `stack up` lease 17 `GRIDIQ_*_PORT` values into the start command's environment. Compose prefers the shell environment over `--env-file`, so leased ports would override the stack file's ports, while the project's readiness checks and `bin/dev-account` read the file. Two allocators would disagree about one stack's ports.
- Declaring `stack` with the project's existing commands works for `/converge`'s drive, but [coding rule 10](plugins/ok/families/ok-planner/docs/plumbline-coding.md#L104-L121) sends every build task through `stack up`. A fixed `start` command then starts one shared stack for every concurrent builder, which take it down under each other. A start command that names the stack after `$RUN_TAG` avoids that, but the project then carries two lifecycles.
- Rule 10 also requires `${OK_RUN_LABEL}` on every compose service, volume, and network, and the lint's `compose-labels` check flags 57 sites across the project's three compose files. The project's own teardown removes its stacks by compose project, so the label adds nothing there.
- True-up keeps the retired `.ok-planner/bin/run-tag` while four project scripts call it, and files one intake issue per caller with no drop-in to repoint to.

The process the suite defines holds for this project: a run gets a fresh tag, isolated ports, a start, a stop, and a cleanup of stale runs. Only the implementation differs.

ruling.text:
Replace the mandated stack tool with optional helpers, and return the process to v25.3.0's model, where each project runs its own stack commands.

1. The process prompts run the project's own commands. `/converge`'s drive and `/audit`'s deployments run the commands that the "Drive commands" section of `.ok-planner/review/project.md` names, as in v25.3.0. No prompt names a suite helper.
2. Remove the mandates: coding rule 10, the cheatsheet's "Per-run artifacts and verification stacks" section, and the lint's `compose-ports` and `compose-labels` checks. `ports` and `port_range` stay only as settings the port registry reads. The `stack` key in `.ok-planner/config.json` stays only as a setting the reference stack tool reads: `.ok-planner/bin/stack up` with no command runs the key's start command, and nothing else in the suite requires the key.
3. Ship helpers that a project may call from its own commands, each usable alone:
   - a tag generator at `.ok-planner/bin/run-tag`, with the same path and output as v25.3.0;
   - a port registry that leases and releases ports per tag, treats a port as taken when it fails to bind over TCP or UDP or when a docker container publishes it, and lists stale leases;
   - a docker sweep that removes every object carrying a run's label or whose compose project equals the run's tag;
   - a process-group helper that starts a command in a group of its own and later stops the group.

   `.ok-planner/bin/stack` stays as a reference start and stop built from the helpers, for a project with no stack tooling of its own.
4. Describe the helpers in a reference document outside the always-loaded rules, with the tag and port advice from v25.3.0's cheatsheet.
5. Each project's own tooling owes the stories `concurrent-stacks-without-port-collisions` and `verification-leaves-no-artifacts-behind`, and `/audit` checks them there.
6. True-up leaves a v26.0.0 project's `stack` key in place, and writes "Drive commands" lines that call the reference stack tool: a `stack-start` line that runs `.ok-planner/bin/stack up` and a `stack-stop` line that runs `.ok-planner/bin/stack down`.

title: The stack lifecycle runs only the suite's own stack tool, so a project with its own stack tooling cannot adopt it

options.label: A
options.text: A project marks, in its review facts, that its instance stories drive one at a time; with the mark, the drives verb files each instance drive after every other driver and chains it after the one before. Cost: one new setting, parsed by the review tool and described in the seed facts file and the converge skill.

options.label: B
options.text: The drives verb always files instance drives one at a time after every other driver, with no setting. Cost: every project with instance stories loses their parallelism, even on hosts with room to spare.

options.label: C
options.text: A numeric limit in the review configuration sets how many instance drives run at once, and the drives verb chains them into that many lanes; a limit of 1 gives option A. Cost: a new configuration key with a seed default and true-up handling, more code than option A.

options.label: D
options.text: Make the drive step's concurrency cap settable per project. Cost: it slows the shared-stack drivers too, and it does not stop instance drives from overlapping each other.

options.label: E
options.text: Leave the drive order as it is. Cost: on a host that cannot fit three stacks, the instance stories are never proven.

problem:
The review tool's drives verb starts every drive that needs a throwaway instance of the product at the same time as the shared-stack drivers, and a project has no way to make those drives wait, so on a host that fits two full stacks but not three the drives time out and the story goes unproven, against [decision:drive-tries-each-story-as-a-user](.ok-planner/design/decisions/drive-tries-each-story-as-a-user.md)'s aim that each run tries every story.

In drive mode and in sprint certification, `/converge` starts one shared product stack and then runs one driver agent per story, up to 8 at once. A project lists its stories under two headings in its review facts file ([seed project.md](plugins/ok/families/ok-planner/review/seed/project.md#L39-L45)). A story under "Stories that drive alone" changes state other drivers read, so it runs after every other driver, one at a time. A story under "Stories that drive on an instance of their own" needs a deployment the shared stack cannot give, so its driver creates a full stack of its own. [review:cmd_drives](plugins/ok/families/ok-planner/scripts/review#L1108) files every story not on the alone list with no ordering ([line 1146](plugins/ok/families/ok-planner/scripts/review#L1146)), instance stories included, and chains only the alone stories after the rest ([lines 1148-1151](plugins/ok/families/ok-planner/scripts/review#L1148-L1151)). The instance list changes only the brief's folder, never the order. [review:story_lists](plugins/ok/families/ok-planner/scripts/review#L1045) refuses a story named under both headings, so a project cannot put an instance story on the alone list to make it wait. The drain loop has one concurrency cap across every task ([drain.md](plugins/ok/families/ok-planner/skills/_tasks/drain.md#L7)) and no limit per kind of drive. [converge SKILL.md step 3](plugins/ok/families/ok-planner/skills/converge/SKILL.md#L78) describes this filing, and step 6 ([line 114](plugins/ok/families/ok-planner/skills/converge/SKILL.md#L114)) chains the confirm drivers the same way.

The GridIQ project hit this on a 16-CPU host with an 8.3 GB Docker VM. Three stacks drove the load average to about 24. The instance's identity provider answered token requests in 10 to 54 seconds, so the drive's CLI sign-in timed out four times while the same drive's browser steps passed. The merge step ([SKILL.md:80](plugins/ok/families/ok-planner/skills/converge/SKILL.md#L80)) sorts such failures as `environment`, so the run reports no false defect, but the story stays unproven on every run on that host. The behavior is unchanged at v26.0.0.

The fix lies in project-owned source: the review tool and the converge skill under `plugins/ok/families/ok-planner/` are this repo's shipped product, and only their materialized copies are suite-owned. No accept-list entry covers the harm, and the corpus says nothing about drive ordering, concurrency, or instances: [decision:stack-tool-runs-each-run](.ok-planner/design/decisions/stack-tool-runs-each-run.md) is silent on concurrent runs on one host. The ruling decides whether and how a project can make its instance-story drives run one at a time after the shared-stack drivers.

recommendation.text:
A project can mark, in its review facts, that its instance stories drive one at a time. With the mark, the drives verb files each instance-story drive after every other driver, the alone stories included, and chains each after the one before, so at most one instance stack runs beside the shared stack. The confirm drivers follow the same order. Without the mark, instance drives keep running beside the shared-stack drivers as they do now.

Rationale: the review facts file already carries the one ordering fact the drive honors, the alone list, so a mark beside the instance list keeps drive ordering in one place and in one idiom, and leaves a project with room to spare its parallelism. Option B costs every project its parallelism for a limit one host shows. Option C buys a lane count no project has asked for, at the price of a new configuration key and its true-up handling. Option D slows the drivers that cause no load and still lets instances overlap. Option E leaves stories unproven, which defeats the drive's purpose. The flip case: if a second project shows that the right limit depends on the machine rather than the project, so that one checkout needs serial drives on a laptop and parallel ones on a larger host, a numeric limit as in option C serves better; if every project that lists instance stories turns out to need them serial, option B removes a setting nobody leaves off.

title: Instance-story drives run beside every shared-stack driver, and a project cannot make them wait

options.text: When the owner drops a file-target type whose target holds a stamped document, the walk asks in the same message whether to remove that document, and removes it only on the owner's word; cost: one more question in the walk, and a kept file returns as untyped documentation at the next walk.

options.label: C
options.text: The goal counts a stamped document at a path no type targets as met; cost: an older release's document stays where readers look, and no one is ever asked about it.

problem:
When the owner drops a document type whose target is a single file, `/document` leaves that type's last document at its target, stamped with an older release, and the run's own goal then fails on it in this release and every later one. That breaks [story:ship-release-documents](.ok-planner/design/stories/ship-release-documents.md), which promises readers 'documentation that describes that release'.

The documentation walk proposes dropping a declared type whose covered classes returned no public element ([document/SKILL.md:Empty types](plugins/ok/families/ok-planner/skills/document/SKILL.md#L132)). Placement then writes only declared targets: 'no path is touched that no type names' ([document/SKILL.md:Placement](plugins/ok/families/ok-planner/skills/document/SKILL.md#L312)). Under a folder target, Placement removes every stamped document no declared type produced this release, 'so a document whose type was dropped does not linger' ([document/SKILL.md:Placement](plugins/ok/families/ok-planner/skills/document/SKILL.md#L314)). No step does the same for a file target. So the dropped type's document stays where readers look, and [document/goal.md](plugins/ok/families/ok-planner/skills/document/goal.md#L83-L87) lists 'a document at a path no type targets' under Not met. The run may not touch that path, so the goal never verifies. The next walk raises the file as untyped documentation ([document/SKILL.md:Untyped documentation](plugins/ok/families/ok-planner/skills/document/SKILL.md#L133)), but its 'drops the file as not documentation' removes nothing either, so only a hand deletion clears it.

A drive in run converge-2026-10-16T040507, the sprint certification of [the stack helpers sprint](.ok-planner/sprints/2026-10-15-stack-helpers.md), found it, and a merge agent confirmed it as real and outside that sprint's scope. Accept-list entry [A3](.ok-planner/review/catalog/accept.md#L11) covers it: an owner's action through a shipped verb leaves a state where later runs fail.

The fix needs a choice, because [decision:documents-generated-per-type-and-placed](.ok-planner/design/decisions/documents-generated-per-type-and-placed.md) commits that 'only declared types' targets are written' and that 'nothing is overwritten that no type claims'. The same decision already allows one removal: the documentation folder's rules file, which the ceremony removes once no type targets that folder. Folder targets are handled; file targets are not.

The ruling decides whether dropping a file-target type removes its stamped document, on the drop alone or on the owner's separate word.
reason: The owner backs out /document and the audit's surface stages until they are redesigned: audit and document both need a rethink (ruling on surface-extraction-completeness-unrecorded).

recommendation.text:
Dropping a file-target type removes the document the ceremony wrote at its target, in the same run, where that document opens with the ceremony's provenance stamp. A file at the target with no stamp is hand-kept and stays. The commitment that the ceremony writes only declared types' targets gains this one removal, beside the removal of the documentation folder's rules file it already allows.

Rationale: the ceremony already removes a dropped type's stamped document under a folder target, so that it does not linger; option A gives a file target the same treatment, and one rule then covers both target shapes. The stamp keeps placement safe: it proves the ceremony wrote the file, and a placed document is a record the next release regenerates whole ([decision:placed-documents-are-records](.ok-planner/design/decisions/placed-documents-are-records.md)), so removing it loses nothing the owner wrote. The owner's drop in the walk is the consent. Option B asks a second time for the same act, and where the owner keeps the file it leaves a stamped orphan the next walk raises again. Option C makes the goal pass while readers still meet an older release's document. Flip case: if owners drop a type to stop regenerating a document they mean to keep by hand, the drop no longer implies removal, and option B, which asks, is the better rule.

ruling.text: Option A

title: A document whose file-target type the owner drops stays in the tree, and the documentation goal can never be met

messages.text: Every judgment an agent makes without the owner counts as a call. That covers a builder's calls, forks, noticed defects, and taken improvements. It also covers certification's declines, not-owed sorts, rejections, and unlisted calls. The completion report lists every call in one table, one row each, with these columns: id, kind, stage or role, site, and a one-line choice. Each agent writes the one-line choice when it records the call. `tasks render` writes the table in place of `## Divergences`. A plain `/converge` run's return lists its declines, not-owed sorts, and rejections in the same table. At the close, the session presents the table, and the owner vetoes any row they disagree with. The session walks nothing else.

options.label: A
options.text: Every judgment a /converge run makes without the owner is a call: the return lists each verified decline, each failure sorted not-owed on one reading, and each report rejected as not real or not covered, one line each with site and reason; cost: a long return block in analysis runs, where rejections are many.

options.label: B
options.text: A call is only what the suite records as a call; the story or a concept says so, and declines, sorts, and rejections stay in the run's ledger; cost: vetoing a decline or a sort takes a ledger read.

options.label: C
options.text: The return lists each verified decline by site and reason, and keeps not-owed sorts and rejections as counts beside the ledger's path; cost: a split rule, and the not-owed sort, the judgment about what the product owes, stays out of the report.

problem:
A `/converge` run's return names three kinds of judgment its agents make without the owner only as counts, or not at all, so an owner who disagrees with one cannot find it from the run's report, though [story:veto-calls-made-in-my-absence](.ok-planner/design/stories/veto-calls-made-in-my-absence.md) promises 'a way to see every call made while I was away, so that I can overturn one I disagree with'.

The three judgments are these. A fixer declines a defect, and a verifier accepts the decline. A merge agent sorts a driver's failure `not-owed` on its one reading of what the product owes. A merge agent rejects a hunter's or a sprint pass's report as not real, or as a harm the accept list does not cover ([converge/prompts/merge.md](plugins/ok/families/ok-planner/skills/converge/prompts/merge.md#L19-L20)). Each agent writes its reason as a note in the run's task ledger under `.ok-planner/review/runs/`. The return ([converge/SKILL.md:The return](plugins/ok/families/ok-planner/skills/converge/SKILL.md#L146-L150)) counts declines on its `fixed` line and counts not-owed and rejected failures on its `hunt` line. Its `intake` line lists rejections only where the file is a record or a document the release regenerates. To overturn any other judgment, the owner must read the ledger.

The run already surfaces a judgment its agent was unsure of: a merge that sees two readings of what the product owes records a question call, and the owner list files it into the intake. A stuck defect becomes a judgment issue. In sprint mode an `unlisted` call goes to the completion report, which records 'what was decided in the owner's absence' for a sprint execution ([concept:completion-report](.ok-planner/design/concepts/completion-report.md)). The gap is a judgment an agent made with confidence: nothing lists it by site and reason.

The corpus never defines 'call', so the story reads two ways: every judgment an agent makes alone, or only what the suite records as a call (the calls pool's items, triage's rulings and closes, a builder's calls). [decision:skill-text-is-reviewed-as-code](.ok-planner/design/decisions/skill-text-is-reviewed-as-code.md) names a fixer that declines a fix apart from one that records a question, and [decision:converge-finds-then-fixes](.ok-planner/design/decisions/converge-finds-then-fixes.md) lets a defect end 'declined with a reason a verifier accepts' without saying whether that decline is a call.

The ruling decides whether each decline, not-owed sort, and report rejection a run makes alone must reach the owner by site and reason.

recommendation.text:
Treat every judgment a `/converge` run makes without the owner as a call the owner can veto. The run's return lists each verified decline, each failure sorted not-owed on one reading, and each report rejected as not real or not covered, one line each with its site and its reason, beside the ledger's path. The counts stay as the summary above those lines.

Rationale: the story promises every call made while the owner was away, and the suite already treats a dismissal made without the owner as one to veto: `/triage-issues` lists each issue it answers or retires in its report for veto, and [decision:closed-issues-leave-new-analysis](.ok-planner/design/decisions/closed-issues-leave-new-analysis.md) relies on a close naming its reason so that a person can veto it. A merge's rejection or not-owed sort is the same act as triage's retire: it dismisses a claim. A not-owed sort judges what the product owes, the judgment the owner most needs to see, so option C hides the wrong half, and option B makes every veto a ledger read. Option A adds one line per judgment. Flip case: if analysis runs routinely reject hundreds of reports, so that the return stops being readable, the return lists declines and not-owed sorts and points to one file that lists every rejection, which still keeps each call findable from the report.

ruling.text: Every judgment an agent makes without the owner counts as a call. That covers a builder's calls, forks, noticed defects, and taken improvements. It also covers certification's declines, not-owed sorts, rejections, and unlisted calls. The completion report lists every call in one table, one row each, with these columns: id, kind, stage or role, site, and a one-line choice. Each agent writes the one-line choice when it records the call. `tasks render` writes the table in place of `## Divergences`. A plain `/converge` run's return lists its declines, not-owed sorts, and rejections in the same table. At the close, the session presents the table, and the owner vetoes any row they disagree with. The session walks nothing else.

title: A /converge run's declines, not-owed sorts, and report rejections reach the owner only as counts

messages.text: Option A

options.label: A
options.text: Wire the chrome-devtools MCP server into this project with `/setup-web`, so every driver session carries a browser tool. Cost: a Chrome install and one more MCP server in every session of the project.

options.label: B
options.text: State in this project's review facts that a drive of the dashboard's page needs a browser tool, and that a driver without one records the page blocked and drives the JSON routes; the existing step 3 sentence changes rather than gains a second one. Cost: the page's controls stay untested.

options.label: C
options.text: Change the drive prompt so a driver whose surface needs a browser, in a session with none, records that surface blocked with the reason at once. Cost: a product change that reaches every consumer project, and it reports the gap without closing it.

options.label: D
options.text: Both A and C: wire the browser tool here, and have the drive prompt report a browser surface blocked wherever a session lacks the tool. Cost: the costs of A and C together.

problem:
A drive of this project never exercises the dashboard's page, because no driver session carries a browser tool, so the page's controls go untested on every run. [decision:drive-tries-each-story-as-a-user](.ok-planner/design/decisions/drive-tries-each-story-as-a-user.md) has a driver try 'every surface the story is offered through', and [decision:local-web-surface](.ok-planner/design/decisions/local-web-surface.md) makes the dashboard a page because working the intake needs 'keys to move through the queue and rule without leaving it'. The mechanism: the drive prompt tells a driver, where a surface runs in a browser, to 'open a page of your own with `new_page`' ([converge/prompts/drive.md](plugins/ok/families/ok-planner/skills/converge/prompts/drive.md#L17)), and names no path for a session without that tool. This project has no `.mcp.json`, so no session carries a browser MCP server. The page is a client-rendered shell, `
` on `GET /`, so only a browser exercises its controls; `curl` reaches only the JSON routes the page calls. The dashboard's drive steps already allow that substitute: step 3 reads 'Drive the page at the service's address, or its JSON routes with `curl`' ([.ok-planner/review/project.md](.ok-planner/review/project.md#L82)). In run converge-2026-10-16T040507 a driver did so: every `POST /api/issue//rule` answered 200, [story:rule-on-the-whole-intake](.ok-planner/design/stories/rule-on-the-whole-intake.md) passed over the routes, and the page's rule keys went undriven. The owner reads a pass that never touched the page. The state of play: the routes are driven, the page is not, and nothing reports the gap. The `/setup-web` skill of the suite's ok-web plugin merges the chrome-devtools MCP server into a project's `.mcp.json`, which gives every session `new_page`. No stated rule decides among the options. The ruling decides what changes so that a drive reaches the page, or reports that it could not.

recommendation.text:
Wire the chrome-devtools MCP server into this project with `/setup-web`, and change the drive prompt so a driver whose surface needs a browser, in a session with no browser tool, records that surface blocked with the reason instead of standing another surface in for it. The dashboard's drive steps then name the page as the surface the story is driven through, and the JSON routes no longer stand in for it.

Rationale: the page is a surface the story is offered through, and its keys are the reason the dashboard is a page rather than a terminal report, so a drive that stops at the routes skips the part the dashboard exists for; only wiring the browser tool (A) closes that gap here. The drive prompt change (C) serves every project the suite ships to: without it, a consumer whose drivers lack a browser tool reads a pass over a page nobody drove, the same false pass this run produced. A statement in the review facts (B) records the gap in one project and leaves the page untested. The flip case: if the machines that run drives cannot install Chrome, A is out, and C with B's statement in the review facts is the right pair.

ruling.text: Option A

title: Drivers cannot drive the dashboard's page because no driver session has a browser tool

messages.text: The stack helpers and the reference stack tool serve a project's stack scripts and the suite's own process, not a person at a terminal. `run-group start` lends no terminal: it runs the command with its input from `/dev/null`, and keeps the caller's output and environment. The terminal-lending code leaves `run-group`, and the reference doc drops its paragraph on Ctrl-C, Ctrl-Z, `bg`, and `fg`. The reference doc says in its opening that the helpers are for scripts to call, not for an owner to run by hand.

options.label: A
options.text: Keep lending: the run's group owns the terminal while its command runs, so Ctrl-C and Ctrl-Z act on the whole run as they act on a shell's foreground job. Cost: a Ctrl-C also ends a background server the operator meant to keep until `stop`.

options.label: B
options.text: Refuse a terminal: `run-group start` refuses where its input, output, or error is a terminal, or runs the command with input from `/dev/null`, so a run's command always runs apart from the operator's terminal. Cost: an interactive command, such as a prompt or a password read, cannot run under run-group, and an operator who runs it by hand must redirect.

options.label: C
options.text: Lend no terminal: the command stays in the run's group, Ctrl-C reaches run-group alone, and run-group forwards SIGINT to the command's own process, so background members run until `stop`. Cost: a command that reads the terminal stops on SIGTTIN, and the forwarding handler is new code.

problem:
When an operator runs `run-group start` at a terminal, it lends the terminal to the run's whole process group, so a Ctrl-C meant for the foreground command also ends every background server the command started. The corpus fixes that every process a run starts sits in the run's process group, and says nothing of what an operator's keystrokes reach.

The mechanism: `start` ([run-group:start](plugins/ok/families/ok-planner/scripts/run-group#L309)) asks [run-group:foreground_terminal](plugins/ok/families/ok-planner/scripts/run-group#L249) whether its input, output, or error is a terminal whose foreground group is run-group's own. Where one is, [run-group:run_lent](plugins/ok/families/ok-planner/scripts/run-group#L296) hands the terminal to the run's group while the command runs, and [run-group:lent_wait](plugins/ok/families/ok-planner/scripts/run-group#L279) takes it back when the command exits, and stops run-group itself when the command stops for any reason but a terminal read, so Ctrl-Z stops run-group as a shell job stops. The holder process that leads the group ignores SIGINT, SIGQUIT, and SIGTSTP ([run-group:HOLD_CODE](plugins/ok/families/ok-planner/scripts/run-group#L66)), so the group outlives a Ctrl-C. A server the command starts with a trailing `&` stays in the group, because `stop` signals the group, so it receives the operator's SIGINT too unless it ignores that signal. The reference doc states this behavior ([docs/stack-helpers.md](plugins/ok/families/ok-planner/docs/stack-helpers.md#L214-L221)). The reference stack tool never meets it, since it runs the start command with input from `/dev/null` and its output to a log ([scripts/stack](plugins/ok/families/ok-planner/scripts/stack#L489)). An operator who runs `run-group start` by hand meets it, and so does a project's own command that calls it at a terminal.

The state of play: [decision:stack-helpers-serve-project-commands](.ok-planner/design/decisions/stack-helpers-serve-project-commands.md) ships run-group as a helper a project may call from its own commands, 'each usable alone', and [decision:run-artifacts-removed-with-the-run](.ok-planner/design/decisions/run-artifacts-removed-with-the-run.md) has `down` stop 'the run's process group'. Running the command outside the run's group would break `stop`, so that reading is no option. No accept-list entry decides the terminal. A choice other than the built one edits the reference doc and run-group's entry in this project's review facts in the same change.

The ruling decides what a run's process group owes an operator at a terminal.

recommendation.text:
Keep lending the terminal to the run's group. While a run's command runs at an operator's terminal, Ctrl-C and Ctrl-Z act on every process of the run but the holder, as they act on a shell's foreground job, and `stop` still removes whatever is left.

Rationale: the corpus makes the run's process group the unit a run is stopped by, so a keystroke that acts on the whole group treats the run as the one thing the corpus says it is; an operator who stops a run's foreground step at a terminal expects the run to stop, not to leave servers running whose only trace is the group. Lending (A) matches the job control every shell user already knows, which suits a helper the corpus ships to be usable alone, and it is built and documented. Refusing a terminal (B) takes away interactive commands to limit a keystroke's reach, and lending no terminal (C) adds a forwarding handler and stops any command that reads the terminal. The flip case: if projects' own commands call `run-group start` at a terminal as a development loop, where the operator ends a foreground step such as a log tail and expects the server to keep running, C fits that use and earns its handler.

ruling.text: The stack helpers and the reference stack tool serve a project's stack scripts and the suite's own process, not a person at a terminal. `run-group start` lends no terminal: it runs the command with its input from `/dev/null`, and keeps the caller's output and environment. The terminal-lending code leaves `run-group`, and the reference doc drops its paragraph on Ctrl-C, Ctrl-Z, `bg`, and `fg`. The reference doc says in its opening that the helpers are for scripts to call, not for an owner to run by hand.

title: run-group start lends the operator's terminal to the whole run, so Ctrl-C also ends the run's background servers

messages.text: Back out `/document` and the audit's surface stages until they are redesigned. Documentation follows a spec that lists the specific documents the project maintains and what each one references. Surface extraction serves only reference document types: which endpoints make up the public API, which CLI tools are part of the public release, and the like. Each sprint updates the documents its work changes, so the documentation stays current without a ceremony at release time. The next `/plan-sprint` plans the redesign.

Back out `/audit` and `/document` until they are redesigned. We don't use the audit at all, and the whole of it gets a rework. Documentation follows a spec that lists the specific documents the project maintains and what each one references. Surface extraction serves only reference document types: which endpoints make up the public API, which CLI tools are part of the public release, and the like. Each sprint updates the documents its work changes, so the documentation stays current without a ceremony at release time. The next `/plan-sprint` plans the redesign.

options.label: A
options.text: Completeness relative to the extraction: the catalog matches the extraction's public side one-to-one, as the documentation skill already says, the surface extraction concept says the walk's exhaustiveness is not promised, and the story is narrowed to say so. Cost: the story's confidence 'without reading the source' rests on a walk nobody can refute.

options.label: B
options.text: Exhaustive enumeration: the extractor records, per kind, the source it enumerated from (the files, registries, or declarations it read) and the count it found there, commits to enumerating every member of that source, and the catalog's population rests on that record, so a later audit can re-enumerate the source and refute a missed element. Cost: the concept's 'nothing else' boundary widens, the extractor's 'no deeper than classification requires' bound changes, and each audit run costs more.

options.label: C
options.text: A named source with no promise: the extractor names, per kind, the source its walk read, in the shape of the audit's count-and-population rule, the concept says only that, and the story reads as completeness relative to the walk. Cost: a reader can check absence against a named source, and nothing promises the source holds every member.

problem:
The documentation catalog counts each public kind against the audit's surface extraction, and the extraction records no population it enumerated from, so an element the audit's walk missed reads as one that does not exist. [story:answer-absence-from-catalogs](.ok-planner/design/stories/answer-absence-from-catalogs.md) promises an agent consuming a release 'every declared user-facing surface kind cataloged completely over its enumerated population', so that it can answer 'does this capability exist?' with confidence from the catalog alone, without reading the source.

The mechanism: the audit dispatches a surface extractor that walks the code and the deployment configuration and writes one entry per element the walk found, each kind discovered by the walk and never pre-declared ([audit/SKILL.md](plugins/ok/families/ok-planner/skills/audit/SKILL.md#L99)). The extractor's rules bound the walk, which 'goes no deeper than classification requires', and ask for no per-kind source or count ([audit/SKILL.md](plugins/ok/families/ok-planner/skills/audit/SKILL.md#L103-L105)). `/document` then writes one catalog file per kind whose `population:` is the count of public members the extraction holds, with rows that 'match the extraction's public side one-to-one' ([document/SKILL.md](plugins/ok/families/ok-planner/skills/document/SKILL.md#L164-L168)), and tells the reader that 'what is not in the catalog does not exist' ([document/SKILL.md](plugins/ok/families/ok-planner/skills/document/SKILL.md#L18)). The catalog's completeness is checked only against the extraction, so nothing a later reader or audit holds can refute an omission the walk made. The agent that consumes the release sees the harm: it answers 'does not exist' with false confidence.

The state of play: the story's 'enumerated population' reads two ways, as the extraction's entries or as an exhaustive enumeration of each kind. [concept:surface-extraction](.ok-planner/design/concepts/surface-extraction.md) says 'one entry per element the walk found' and that the extraction 'states what the walk found and how the intent classified it — nothing else', which decides neither. The nearest stated rule, 'Every universal comes back as a count and its population ... report the number checked and where the set came from' ([artifact-definitions.md](.claude/skills/_shared/artifact-definitions.md#L358)), governs audit records, not the extraction. Two open defect issues, document-catalog-per-declared-kind and document-goal-skips-catalog-completeness, fix the catalog to one file per extraction kind with rows one-to-one with the extraction; their fixes hold under every option here.

The ruling decides what completeness the catalog owes: completeness relative to the walk, or completeness over a population the extraction records.

recommendation.text:
The surface extraction commits to exhaustive enumeration per kind. For each kind it records the source it enumerated from, such as the files, registries, or declarations it read, and the count it found there, and it enumerates every member of that source. The catalog's population for each kind rests on that record, and an audit can re-enumerate a named source to refute a missed element. The story stands as written.

Rationale: the story is the owner's promise, and it promises an agent confidence in absence without reading the source. Exhaustive enumeration (B) keeps that promise, where relative completeness (A) narrows it and a named source with no promise (C) records where the set came from while committing to nothing about it. The project already answers every universal claim with a count and where the set came from, in audit records and in a subject's coverage, whose population is enumerated from the code; the catalog's 'what is not in the catalog does not exist' is such a universal, and B gives it the same shape. The extractor already visits each element to classify it, so naming the source and its count adds a record more than a walk. The flip case: if some kinds have no finite source a walk can name, such as environment variables read through computed names, exhaustiveness cannot be shown for them; C is then the honest commitment for those kinds, with the story narrowed to match.

ruling.text: Back out `/audit` and `/document` until they are redesigned. We don't use the audit at all, and the whole of it gets a rework. Documentation follows a spec that lists the specific documents the project maintains and what each one references. Surface extraction serves only reference document types: which endpoints make up the public API, which CLI tools are part of the public release, and the like. Each sprint updates the documents its work changes, so the documentation stays current without a ceremony at release time. The next `/plan-sprint` plans the redesign.

title: The documentation catalog is complete only over what the audit's surface walk happened to find

Where the review facts file does not decode as UTF-8, true-up files an intake issue for the owner, says in its report that it filed one, and leaves the file as it stands. The issue names the file, says that true-up cannot read or rewrite it, and names the retired review tool's path and the path that replaces it.

Rationale: an intake issue with the file left is the shape the corpus already gives a retired reference true-up cannot rewrite, and the shape the same core already uses for an undecodable caller of a retired script, so the core keeps one idiom for one job (B). It ends the silent default the coding rules forbid with a record the owner works through the intake, where a `stale:` line (C) scrolls past and repeats on every true-up. A byte rewrite (A) answers with no question, and it adds a second idiom beside the never-rewrite rule and can corrupt a file in an encoding it does not read. The flip case: if undecodable review facts files prove common, one issue per project becomes noise, and true-up should instead detect the file's encoding and rewrite it in that encoding.

options.label: A
options.text: Rewrite the ASCII name byte for byte in the raw bytes. Cost: a second idiom beside the core's rule that it never rewrites an undecodable file, and a wrong edit in an encoding where those bytes do not stand for the name, such as UTF-16.

options.label: B
options.text: File an intake issue for the owner and leave the file, as the caller scan does for an undecodable caller of a retired script. Cost: one more issue for the owner, on a rare file.

options.label: C
options.text: Print a `stale:` line naming the file from both check and fix, with no write and no issue. Cost: a notice the owner must act on unprompted, which every true-up repeats and nothing records.

problem:
True-up silently skips the review facts file, `.ok-planner/review/project.md`, when it does not decode as UTF-8, so a retired `.ok-review/bin/review` in that file is neither rewritten nor reported. [decision:whole-file-ownership](.ok-planner/design/decisions/whole-file-ownership.md) has true-up rewrite a value in owner-declared configuration that names a retired estate's path with no offer, and, for a retired script line it cannot rewrite, file an intake issue for the owner and leave the line. Rule 4.6 of [plumbline-coding.md](.claude/rules/plumbline-coding.md) says 'A caught error never ends in a bare log line or a silent default'.

The mechanism: [admin/true-up:review_config_mode](plugins/ok/families/ok-planner/admin/true-up#L3692) reads the file and, on `UnicodeDecodeError`, returns with no line printed ([admin/true-up](plugins/ok/families/ok-planner/admin/true-up#L3718)), so neither the check step's `stale:` line nor the fix step's rewrite to `.ok-planner/bin/review` happens. The stale-wording scan cannot catch it: [admin/true-up:wording_left](plugins/ok/families/ok-planner/admin/true-up#L2377) strips `.ok-review/bin/review` before [admin/true-up:stale_wording_lines](plugins/ok/families/ok-planner/admin/true-up#L2384) looks for a retired estate path, because `review_config_mode` owns that name. The stack-lines offer names the decode failure only where `.ok-planner/config.json` declares a stack ([admin/true-up:stack_plan](plugins/ok/families/ok-planner/admin/true-up#L3227)), drops it for a seeded skeleton ([admin/true-up:stack_lines_offers](plugins/ok/families/ok-planner/admin/true-up#L3281)), and never names the retired review tool. `/converge` pastes the review facts into every prompt, so once the retired estate is gone, an agent told to run the review tool by that path meets a missing file.

The state of play: the same core already handles an undecodable file elsewhere. Its scan for callers of a retired script classifies such a caller as kind `encoding`, 'a file that does not decode as UTF-8, so true-up cannot rewrite it byte for byte' ([admin/true-up](plugins/ok/families/ok-planner/admin/true-up#L1801)), and files an intake issue for it ([admin/true-up:caller_issue](plugins/ok/families/ok-planner/admin/true-up#L1925)). The built silent skip breaks rule 4.6, so keeping it is no option; the choice lies among the rest.

The ruling decides what true-up owes an owner whose review facts file does not decode.

messages.text:
Count every message on an open issue, a person's comment or ruling included, as unread to each person except its author until that person next reads the issue, on the command line and the dashboard alike. Reading an issue marks every message on it read, not only the agent messages. A message counts once, by its number, so an edit or withdrawal of a message the reader already read does not count again. The tooling text that describes unread counts says the same.

Rationale: the story promises new answers 'whoever wrote them', and the corpus already builds for several people working one intake: [decision:read-marks-kept-per-person](.ok-planner/design/decisions/read-marks-kept-per-person.md) gives each person a ledger so that one person's reading never clears another's, and [decision:unread-issues-count-as-new](.ok-planner/design/decisions/unread-issues-count-as-new.md) counts a never-read issue as new whoever filed it. A second person's answer is the new material a shared intake exists to carry. Option B narrows the story to fit the code, and option C leaves a comment that answers a question unseen. The larger counts option A brings are the signal the story asks for. Flip case: where one owner and the agents work the intake and no second person's message ever arrives, option B costs nothing and keeps the code as it stands; where people's comments flood the unread tab in practice, option C keeps the count to rulings.

options.label: A
options.text: Every message, people's comments and rulings included, counts as unread to each person except its author, on the command line and the dashboard; cost: unread counts grow in a busy intake several people work.

options.label: B
options.text: The story's 'whoever wrote them' means whichever agent or ceremony: the story is narrowed to say so, and only agent messages count as unread; cost: one person's answer reaches another person only when that person rereads the issue.

options.label: C
options.text: A person's ruling counts as unread to every other person, and a person's comment does not; cost: a third rule to explain, and a comment that answers a question still goes unseen.

problem:
The intake counts only agent messages as unread, so a comment or ruling one person writes never shows as new to another person, though [story:see-new-analysis](.ok-planner/design/stories/see-new-analysis.md) promises a way to see which open issues 'have new answers or revisions since I last read them, whoever wrote them'.

The intake module decides what is unread for both surfaces that show it. [issues:unread_message](plugins/ok/families/ok-planner/scripts/issues#L510) counts a message only where it is a triage reply or an agent update ([issues:AGENT_TYPE_AUTHORS](plugins/ok/families/ok-planner/scripts/issues#L54)). When a person reads an issue, [issues:mark_read](plugins/ok/families/ok-planner/scripts/issues#L1200) sets that person's read mark to the highest agent message number ([issues:agent_mark](plugins/ok/families/ok-planner/scripts/issues#L502)), not the highest message number. `issues list --unread` and the dashboard's unread tab both count through these functions. So when bob comments on an issue alice has already read, alice's `issues list --unread` prints nothing, and the dashboard's `GET /api/issues?unread=1` answers an empty list. The sprint certification of [the stack helpers sprint](.ok-planner/sprints/2026-10-15-stack-helpers.md), run converge-2026-10-16T040507, observed both.

The corpus leans two ways. The story says 'whoever wrote them'. [decision:unread-issues-count-as-new](.ok-planner/design/decisions/unread-issues-count-as-new.md) counts a never-read issue as new 'whoever filed it', and [decision:read-marks-kept-per-person](.ok-planner/design/decisions/read-marks-kept-per-person.md) keeps one ledger per person so that one person's reading never clears another's. But [decision:agent-revisions-reach-the-owner](.ok-planner/design/decisions/agent-revisions-reach-the-owner.md) commits only to agent revisions, 'whichever ceremony writes it', and says nothing of people's messages. The tooling text states the narrow behavior: [the planner's CLAUDE.md template](plugins/ok/families/ok-planner/scripts/ok-planner-CLAUDE.md#L391-L392) says each triage reply and agent revision stays unread to you, and [project.md](.ok-planner/review/project.md#L33) describes `--unread` as listing open issues with agent messages you have not read.

A never-read issue and every agent message already count. Nothing counts a person's comment or ruling. Counting them takes three changes together: the unread test admits people's messages, the read mark covers every message, and a person's own messages never count as unread to that person.

The ruling decides whether a person's comment or ruling counts as unread to every other person who works the intake.

options.label: A
options.text: A sprint may carry a work item, approved by the owner at sign-off, that retires an existing suite: its build task first moves each fitness check that enforces a written rule into a lint check or an assertion, then deletes the suite. Amend decision:tests-forbidden to drop 'never deleted' and the claim that ignoring a suite costs nothing. Cost: a new kind of work item, and moving each fitness check is real work.

options.label: B
options.text: True-up offers to retire every existing suite as a destructive step under the owner's one consent, and lists each fitness check it deletes so the owner can give the rule a new check. Cost: a rule whose check the owner never moves goes unchecked, and true-up takes on judgment about test content.

options.label: C
options.text: Keep the rule. Amend decision:tests-forbidden to say that the owner deletes a suite by hand, outside any agent, and that a toolchain which compiles tests makes a kept suite block removals. Cost: the owner does the deletion and the fitness-check moves alone, with no help from the suite.

problem:
The ok suite's no-tests rule forbids every agent to delete an existing test suite, and nothing in the suite retires one. A project whose owner wants an old suite gone cannot remove it through the suite's own process, and the kept suite blocks product changes in the meantime.

[decision:tests-forbidden](.ok-planner/design/decisions/tests-forbidden.md) says an existing suite "stays where it is, never deleted and never consulted", because "ignoring it costs nothing". The cheatsheet every agent reads says "Never delete one either" ([plumbline-cheatsheet](plugins/ok/families/ok-planner/docs/plumbline-cheatsheet.md#L110)).

Ignoring a suite costs something in two ways. First, many toolchains compile test files during lint or build: golangci-lint type-checks Go test files by default. Deleting or renaming code that a test imports then fails the project's required lint, and the agent may neither fix the test nor delete it. Second, a suite often holds fitness checks that enforce written rules, such as module boundaries or a port registry. Agents never run them, so those rules go unchecked, and the suite has no step that moves a check into the lint.

A Go project under ok-planner v27.0.0 shows both. Its owner chose to drop a database driver. 49 test files outside the driver import its package, so deleting the package fails lint. The same tree holds 35 fitness checks under test paths. The owner then chose to remove every existing suite and found that the rules forbid the step.

The ruling decides whether the suite lets an owner retire an existing suite, and how.
reason: Can an owner retire an existing test suite through the suite's own process? decision:legacy-suites-sorted-automatically settles it: a project's first test sprint sorts every legacy test, and a test that enforces a written rule "is ported: a port task rewrites it as a project check outside the test paths, adds it to the review loop's `checks`, and deletes the test", while an orphan "is deleted"; decision:tests-forbidden is gone, replaced by decision:test-sprints-own-the-tests, and the cheatsheet now says "Only a test sprint adds, edits, or deletes a test."
title: The no-tests rule keeps every existing test suite and offers no way to retire one

`/discover-design` files each request to read more code that its Phase 2 reviewer still makes after the run's one re-read as an issue for the owner. The owner's queue then holds reading chores where the skill promises judgment questions.

`/discover-design` builds a design corpus from a project's code in two phases. Phase 1 writes notes on the code, and Phase 2 writes the corpus from the notes. Phase 2's reviewer may report a thin discovery request: a note too thin to support an artifact, where the fix is to read more code. Its prompt counts only a read-more-code fix as such a request, and sends a fix that needs a design decision to the owner as an issue. The run then makes one back-edge: it re-reads the code each request names and rewrites the affected artifacts. Step 6c sends the reviewer over them once more and files its findings, and any thin request it still makes, as issues. The project's issue definition says to fix mechanical findings in the cycle and file none. The harm is the thin requests alone; the reviewer's other findings stay filed.

The skill serves [story:bootstrap-design-corpus](.ok-planner/design/stories/bootstrap-design-corpus.md), which promises 'a queue of judgment questions, so that my design attention is spent resolving genuine ambiguities'. [decision:intake-writers-are-gated](.ok-planner/design/decisions/intake-writers-are-gated.md#L76) calls what the run files 'the queue of judgment questions it hands back'.

A merge agent of the Oct 17 sprint certification confirmed the defect, outside that sprint's scope. The skill released in v28.0.0, and this project's installed copy, still carry step 6c. A rewrite of the skill's source, staged in the working tree but not committed, drops the back-edge and files no issue.
