problem.before:
When sprint certification fixes a defect and the fix changes something a user can observe, such as a flag, a message, or an output format, no agent brings along the documentation that describes it, so the sprint's commit ships documentation of the behavior before the fix. That breaks the promise that each change brings the documentation it affects along in the same change, so the documentation at any commit describes the product at that commit ([story:keep-documentation-current](.ok-planner/design/stories/keep-documentation-current.md)).

The mechanism. A docspec is the owner's declaration of one kind of documentation: where it lives, and which parts of the project it describes ([concept:docspec](.ok-planner/design/concepts/docspec.md)). A change reaches a docspec two ways ([artifact-definitions.md](plugins/ok/families/ok-planner/skills/_shared/artifact-definitions.md#L172-L173)): it touches a file the docspec's references name, or it touches a file the surface intent names as declaring a class of public element the docspec must list in full. Certification's review runs its documentation passes once, before any fix ([converge/SKILL.md](plugins/ok/families/ok-planner/skills/converge/SKILL.md#L101)). That pass ([sprint-pass.md](plugins/ok/families/ok-planner/skills/converge/prompts/sprint-pass.md#L28)) covers both reach paths and reports each public element the documentation omits. After the review, the fixer is told 'Change nothing the defect does not need' ([fix.md](plugins/ok/families/ok-planner/skills/converge/prompts/fix.md#L24)) and has no step that reads a docspec, and the verifier checks 'the change, and only the change' ([verify.md](plugins/ok/families/ok-planner/skills/converge/prompts/verify.md#L9)). The next `/plan-sprint` reconciles only changes made after the sprint's closing commit ([decision:closing-commit-baseline](.ok-planner/design/decisions/closing-commit-baseline.md)), so nothing later catches the stale text. A reader of the documentation at that commit sees it.

The state of play. A kept fix in the certification run converge-2026-10-17T021110 widened the rule for which prose is in review: documentation a sprint's change reaches, its certification fixes included, is now in review ([coding-rules.md:PROSE-SCOPE-RULE](plugins/ok/families/ok-planner/skills/_converge/coding-rules.md#L38-L61), restated at [converge/SKILL.md](plugins/ok/families/ok-planner/skills/converge/SKILL.md#L40)). So the documentation is in scope, but no agent reads it after a fix. A second fix gave the fixer and the verifier a documentation step over the references path only. The confirm driver sent it back because it missed the declaring-file path and caught only sentences a fix made false, not public elements a fix added, and the run backed it out. The decision on who writes documentation ([decision:sprints-write-the-documentation](.ok-planner/design/decisions/sprints-write-the-documentation.md)) says certification reviews each touched documentation against its docspec and the change, and says nothing of certification fixes. Three sibling issues bear on the same rule and are best ruled together: converge-commits-leave-documentation-behind, for plain runs; listed-class-change-reach, on how a declaring-file change reaches a docspec; and out-of-band-review-misses-declaring-files.

after.text:
A certification fixer whose change alters what a user sees updates the documentation of every docspec the change reaches, by either path. It rewrites each sentence the fix made false and adds each public element the fix added. It follows the one statement of the reach rule and the listing rule the suite already carries, not a second copy. The verifier checks the documentation as part of the change. Rule listed-class-change-reach in the same sprint, so the declaring-file path means the same thing here as at planning.

Rationale: the documentation decision has the agent who writes a change write its documentation after the code, and has review judge both. A gives a certification fix that same shape. A also keeps the fix loop as the decision on finding and fixing defines it: the verifier reads only the change, which now includes its documentation. B reuses the review's check but re-reads after the fix loop, which that decision rejected for code, so B needs that decision amended. C gives up the story's promise of current documentation at any commit, for every sprint whose certification changes behavior. The backed-out attempt failed on its scope, one reach path and false sentences only, not on its shape, and A closes both gaps. The flip case: if the fixer and the verifier cannot apply the listing rule by reference, A would copy the documentation pass's listing procedure into the fix and verify prompts, and then B's single check is the better call despite the amendment.

title: Sprint certification fixes never update the documentation they change

options.label: A
options.text: [decision:sprints-write-the-documentation](.ok-planner/design/decisions/documentation-sprints-write-the-documentation.md) admits a `/converge` fix that brings along the documentation its change reaches, and the run's scope rule, fix, and verify steps widen to match; cost: every plain run reads the docspecs and the surface intent and edits documentation, by whatever mechanism the ruling on certification-fix-leaves-documentation settles.

options.label: B
options.text: [story:keep-documentation-current](.ok-planner/design/stories/keep-documentation-current.md) scopes 'at any commit' to the commits a sprint makes, and a plain run's commits wait for the next reconcile; cost: the documentation is stale from a plain run's commit until the next sprint, and the story promises less.

options.label: C
options.text: As B, and a plain run's owner list files an issue naming each docspec a committed fix reached, so the gap is recorded at the commit instead of found at reconcile; cost: the documentation is still stale until the next sprint, and each reached docspec costs one intake write.

problem:
A plain `/converge` run, in drive, analysis, or defects mode, commits product fixes and leaves the documentation those fixes affect as it was. That breaks the promise of [story:keep-documentation-current](.ok-planner/design/stories/keep-documentation-current.md): 'each change to my product bring the documentation it affects along in the same change, so that the documentation a reader finds at any commit describes the product at that commit.'

The mechanism: such a run fixes product code and ends with an offer to commit the fixes. Its prose scope rule, [{{PROSE-SCOPE-RULE}}](plugins/ok/families/ok-planner/skills/_converge/coding-rules.md#L38-L61), puts documentation in review only in a run that certifies a sprint: 'Anywhere else, and in a run that certifies no sprint, file no finding on it and edit none of it.' The rule follows [decision:sprints-write-the-documentation](.ok-planner/design/decisions/documentation-sprints-write-the-documentation.md), whose Choice reads 'Of the suite's runs, only a sprint writes a project's documentation' and 'Outside these, documentation stays as it is.' A docspec is the owner's declaration of one kind of documentation and the parts of the project it describes ([concept:docspec](.ok-planner/design/concepts/docspec.md)). So a fix that changes a flag, a message, or an output that a docspec's documentation describes lands in a commit whose documentation still describes the old behavior, and every reader of that documentation sees the old behavior until something catches it up.

The state of play: a catch-up path exists. The next `/plan-sprint`'s reconcile flags 'Code or corpus a docspec references, changed outside a sprint' and adds a work item or an issue ([decision:out-of-band-documentation-reconciled](.ok-planner/design/decisions/out-of-band-documentation-reconciled.md)). So the documentation is wrong from the plain run's commit until the next sprint, and no longer. The story and the decision cannot both hold for a plain run's commits, and either fix changes the corpus, so no review run could make it: converge-2026-10-17T021110 left it alone. The sibling issue certification-fix-leaves-documentation asks the same question of a fix made during sprint certification, where documentation is already in review, and its attempted fix stuck on how a fixer finds every docspec a change reaches. This project declares no docspec yet, so the harm reaches consumer projects, not this tree today.

The ruling decides whether a plain run brings the documentation its fixes reach along in the same commit, or the story's promise narrows to the commits a sprint makes.
reason: Commit 554b441 moved all documentation work into documentation sprints; a plain /converge run writes no documentation, and the next documentation sprint's window, opened from each docspec's stamp, catches the change. The owner closed it in /plan-sprint on 2026-10-22.

recommendation.text:
A plain `/converge` run brings along the documentation its fixes reach, in the same commit, by the same mechanism the ruling on certification-fix-leaves-documentation adopts for certification fixes. The decision that only a sprint writes documentation admits that run as a second writer, and the run's verifiers judge its documentation edits as they judge its code edits.

Rationale: the story promises documentation that is current at every commit, not at every sprint. Option B gives that up for the plain runs that change product behavior between sprints, and option C only records the loss. The decision's own rationale is that a change and its documentation land together and a reviewer judges both; a `/converge` run already has a verifier reading each change, so admitting it keeps the decision's reason while it widens the list of writers. One mechanism for both kinds of run keeps one idiom for bringing documentation along, and the reconcile at planning stays as the net for edits no run made. The flip case: if the sibling ruling leaves a certification fix's documentation to the next sprint, or reading the docspecs and the surface intent on every plain fix costs more than the drift it prevents, B with C's recorded gap is the consistent call.

title: A plain /converge run commits fixes that leave the documentation describing the old behavior

options.label: A
options.text: Reach is derived, as built: a change under a file the surface intent names as declaring a listed class, or a surface intent change to such a class, reaches the docspec, and the three decisions' matching sentences say so; cost: every matcher reads the surface intent and each `## Lists` beside the index.

options.label: B
options.text: Reach is declared: a reference docspec's References must name the declaring files of every class it lists, review enforces it, and matching reads references alone; cost: a surface intent change that reclassifies a class, or a declaring file the intent adds later, reaches no docspec until a docspec change follows, so the reference can go stale silently.

options.label: C
options.text: As B, and every reference docspec with `## Lists` names the surface intent itself among its References, so every surface intent change reaches it; cost: every surface intent change touches every reference docspec, even one whose classes it leaves alone, and a declaring file added later is still missed.

problem:
The design corpus does not say how a change to a class of public surface that a reference docspec lists reaches that docspec, and the tooling builds a reading the corpus's matching sentences do not state. [story:reference-names-the-public-surface](.ok-planner/design/stories/reference-names-the-public-surface.md), which owes a reference naming 'every element I made public and no element I kept internal', and [story:keep-documentation-current](.ok-planner/design/stories/keep-documentation-current.md), which owes documentation that moves 'in the same change', rest on that unratified reading.

Background: a docspec declares one kind of documentation. Its `## References` name the corpus artifacts and code paths the documentation describes, and a reference docspec's `## Lists` names the classes of public surface it must list ([concept:docspec](.ok-planner/design/concepts/docspec.md)). The surface intent says which classes are public and names the files that declare each class's members ([decision:surface-members-listed-at-need](.ok-planner/design/decisions/surface-members-listed-at-need.md)). A generated index carries each docspec's location and references, so planning matches drafted work in one read ([decision:one-docspec-per-file](.ok-planner/design/decisions/one-docspec-per-file.md)).

The mechanism: the corpus's matching sentences name references alone. [decision:sprints-write-the-documentation](.ok-planner/design/decisions/documentation-sprints-write-the-documentation.md) says planning 'matches the drafted work against each docspec's references'; one-docspec-per-file says the same of the index; [decision:out-of-band-documentation-reconciled](.ok-planner/design/decisions/out-of-band-documentation-reconciled.md) flags 'Code or corpus a docspec references, changed outside a sprint'. A new command added to a declaring file, or a surface intent change that makes a class public, changes what a reference must list without touching any path its References name. Read by the corpus's words, the reference goes stale with nothing noticing.

The state of play: a fixer built the derived reading at every matcher but one. The docspec definition's [## Lists bullet](plugins/ok/families/ok-planner/skills/_shared/artifact-definitions.md#L173), planning's documentation match, the code planner's Docspecs line and step 8, and the certification reading's step 6 each count a change under a listed class's declaring file, or a surface intent delta that changes such a class's rule, an exception, or its declaring line. The out-of-band reviewer's test at core.md:121-122 still names references alone; the sibling defect out-of-band-review-misses-declaring-files follows from this ruling, and the stuck defect certification-fix-leaves-documentation rests on it. This repository keeps no docspec or surface intent, so the question concerns the shipped tooling.

The ruling decides whether a listed class reaches its docspec through the surface intent, as built, or only through paths each docspec declares in its References.
reason: scripts/docs derives reach from the surface intent: it reports 'declaring file changed' for a change under a listed class's declaring file and 'surface intent changed' for a change to the intent. The owner closed it in /plan-sprint on 2026-10-22.

recommendation.text:
Reach is derived from the surface intent, as built. A change under a file the surface intent names as declaring a class a docspec lists, or a surface intent change to such a class's rule, exceptions, or declaring files, reaches that docspec, and every matcher applies both paths: planning, code planning, certification, and the out-of-band reconcile. The generated docspec index projects each listed class's declaring files from the surface intent beside the docspec's references, so a matcher still answers the match from one read.

Rationale: the surface intent is the one place that names declaring files, and [decision:surface-members-listed-at-need](.ok-planner/design/decisions/surface-members-listed-at-need.md) and [decision:surface-intent-is-one-prose-document](.ok-planner/design/decisions/surface-intent-is-one-prose-document.md) reject a second stored copy of the surface because it drifts. B and C make every reference docspec repeat the declaring files, and B fails silently on the change the story most needs caught, a class made public. Generating the index from both sources keeps one-docspec-per-file's one-read match while the index stays a projection, never a copy. The flip case: if the owner wants each docspec to state in one file everything that reaches it, auditable by eye, and accepts a review check that its References cover its listed classes' declaring files, B is the call; C adds churn without closing B's gap.

title: How a change to a class a reference docspec lists reaches that docspec

options.label: A
options.text: Reach is derived, per option A of listed-class-change-reach: the out-of-band reviewer also reads each docspec's `## Lists` and the surface intent, and flags a change outside a sprint under a file the intent names as declaring a listed class; the reconcile outcome and [decision:out-of-band-documentation-reconciled](.ok-planner/design/decisions/out-of-band-documentation-reconciled.md) name that change beside a change to a referenced file; cost: the reviewer reads two more inputs, and the decision takes a delta.

options.label: B
options.text: Reach is declared, per option B of listed-class-change-reach: each reference docspec's `## References` names the declaring file of every class it lists, so the reviewer's existing test already flags the change, and the reviewer stays as it is; cost: nothing here beyond that issue's own, under which a declaring file the surface intent adds later reaches no docspec until someone amends References.

problem:
Planning's reconcile step does not flag a change made outside a sprint to a file that declares a class of public surface a reference docspec lists, so the reference can go stale with nothing noticing, against [story:reference-names-the-public-surface](.ok-planner/design/stories/reference-names-the-public-surface.md), which owes a reference that names every public element and no internal one.

The mechanism. A docspec orders one piece of documentation. A docspec for reference documentation carries a `## Lists` section that names classes of public surface, and the surface intent names, for each class, the files that declare its members. At the start of each `/plan-sprint`, an out-of-band reviewer reads every change since the last closed sprint and flags the ones the owner must decide. Its inputs ([plan-sprint/core.md](plugins/ok/families/ok-planner/skills/plan-sprint/core.md#L94-L101)) are the docspec index and each docspec's `## Where` and `## References`, never `## Lists` or the surface intent. Its test ([plan-sprint/core.md:The test](plugins/ok/families/ok-planner/skills/plan-sprint/core.md#L115-L136)) flags an edit to documentation and a change to a corpus artifact or code path a docspec's References names, and the matching outcome in [plan-sprint/SKILL.md](plugins/ok/families/ok-planner/skills/plan-sprint/SKILL.md#L77) reads 'Code or a corpus artifact a docspec references, changed outside a sprint'. A commit that adds a public command in a declaring file that References does not also name therefore passes as ambient. No sprint names the docspec, so no builder rewrites the reference, and a reader depends on a list that omits the new command.

The state of play. Inside a sprint, reach is derived: the docspec definition's `## Lists` bullet ([_shared/artifact-definitions.md](plugins/ok/families/ok-planner/skills/_shared/artifact-definitions.md#L173)), planning's documentation match ([plan-sprint/SKILL.md](plugins/ok/families/ok-planner/skills/plan-sprint/SKILL.md)), and certification's reading ([_sprint/shared.md](plugins/ok/families/ok-planner/skills/_sprint/shared.md)) each count a change under a listed class's declaring file, or a surface intent delta to such a class, as reaching the docspec. A direct edit to the surface intent outside a sprint is already always flagged. Only an out-of-band change to a declaring file goes unflagged. [decision:out-of-band-documentation-reconciled](.ok-planner/design/decisions/out-of-band-documentation-reconciled.md) names only 'Code or corpus a docspec references', and the reviewer follows those words, so whether this is a defect turns on the open issue listed-class-change-reach: whether reach is derived from the surface intent or declared in each docspec's References.

recommendation.text:
Rule this with listed-class-change-reach, and take derived reach in both. The out-of-band reviewer flags a change made outside a sprint to a file the surface intent names as declaring a class some reference docspec lists, as it flags a change to a referenced file, and the owner decides it with the same two outcomes: a work item updates the documentation, or an issue defers it. The decision on out-of-band documentation names that change beside a change to what a docspec references.

Rationale: planning's documentation match, code planning, the docspec definition, and certification already derive reach from the surface intent, so option A makes the out-of-band reviewer match the way every other matcher matches, under the [one idiom per job](.claude/rules/plumbline-cheatsheet.md) rule. options.label: A
options.text: Restate the Tests section positively at the moment the habit fires: when a change touches behavior a test may check, the agent reads the design corpus and drives the product, and treats every test as stale output a test sprint owns. The rule names the acts it replaces: searching tests for selectors or strings, keeping a test passing, and reporting a broken test.

options.label: B
options.text: Enforce the read half: a hook refuses a Read or a search whose path matches a test path while no test sprint is open, as the edit hook refuses a write.

options.label: C
options.text: Both A and B.

problem:
The rule that forbids reading tests as evidence does not stop an agent that has it loaded. The agent's training treats a project's tests as the spec of its behavior, and the rule states only prohibitions, so at the moment the habit fires nothing in the rule tells the agent where to look instead. Outside a test sprint, the agent searches the tests, shapes its change to keep them passing, and reports broken tests as work to do. Each of those acts treats a test as evidence, which the rule forbids.

The rule is the Tests section of [plumbline-cheatsheet.md](plugins/ok/families/ok-planner/docs/plumbline-cheatsheet.md), which every consumer project loads as `.claude/rules/plumbline-cheatsheet.md`: "Outside a test sprint's tasks, add no test, edit no test, delete no test, and read no test as evidence." [decision:test-sprints-own-the-tests](.ok-planner/design/decisions/test-sprints-own-the-tests.md) makes the same choice. The lint's `no-tests` check and the edit hook enforce only the write half: they refuse an added or modified file at a test path. Nothing enforces the read half.

A consumer project, verantel, showed the failure on 2026-10-21 in a session that had the rule loaded. During a restyle of the staff dashboard, a change outside any test sprint, the session searched the end-to-end tests for the button text, field ids, and table elements they select. It then told four build subagents to keep those exact strings and ids. At the close it reported a broken end-to-end test, whose link text the restyle had changed, as work for a test sprint. When the owner asked whether a rule against this existed, the session quoted the rule and said it had broken it twice. The owner judged the cause to be the agent's training, not a missing rule, and asked for a framing of the rule that holds against that training.

The harm: a change outside a test sprint bends to keep stale tests passing, so the tests steer product decisions the design corpus and the drive are meant to make. The agent's report then sends test work to the owner that the next test sprint finds on its own.

The ruling decides how the suite states or enforces the read half of the rule so that it holds against an agent's trained habit.
reason: Commit e9949f9 restates the Tests section of plugins/ok/families/ok-planner/docs/plumbline-cheatsheet.md per the owner's ruling (option A): it names the three acts that treat a test as evidence and says what to do in place of each. Consumer projects receive it on their next /ok true-up.

No read hook for now; we try A and see how it goes. The reworded section is staged in plugins/ok/families/ok-planner/docs/plumbline-cheatsheet.md.

problem.after:
`/plan-sprint` reads an upstream ruling as a choice to file only when the ruling names where the owner filed. So when an owner accepts a recommendation to file, before filing, the next planning session calls the ruling unclear and asks the owner to rule again.

An upstream issue names a harm whose fix lies in a part the project does not own, such as a suite-owned file. Triage recommends one of three answers: a workaround in the project, filing a ready draft with the part's maintainers, or both. One key on the dashboard accepts the recommendation and writes its text, such as 'File the draft with the ok suite.', as the ruling. At its start, `/plan-sprint` closes an upstream issue whose ruling names where the draft was filed, and turns a ruling that names a workaround into sprint work. It treats any other ruling as one it cannot understand.

A ruling given before the filing can choose to file but cannot say where. The owner ruled in one sitting, yet the next session opens with a question, against the promise of [story:rule-on-the-whole-intake](.ok-planner/design/stories/rule-on-the-whole-intake.md) that the session 'starts with no question left unanswered'. The session still needs the filing's location to close the issue, as [decision:foreign-harms-become-upstream-issues](.ok-planner/design/decisions/foreign-harms-become-upstream-issues.md) says, but the owner reports that location as a fact after filing; it is not a second ruling.

A driver accepted such a recommendation on the dashboard during a sprint certification, and a merge agent confirmed the defect.

problem.after:
Sprint certification's return, the block it writes when a sprint closes, gives a line for each work item and none for the sprint's corpus deltas. The owner sees a count of landed deltas once, at the close, and the completion report keeps none of it.

A sprint carries two kinds of approved content. Work items are changes builders make to the code. Corpus deltas are the final text of each design artifact the sprint changes: a concept, story, decision, docspec, or the surface intent. After the build, sprint certification reviews the change. Its alignment pass compares each delta with its artifact byte for byte ([converge/prompts/sprint-pass.md](plugins/ok/families/ok-planner/skills/converge/prompts/sprint-pass.md#L27)). A delta that did not land becomes a defect, and a fixer lands it by copying the delta's text into place ([converge/prompts/fix.md](plugins/ok/families/ok-planner/skills/converge/prompts/fix.md#L27)).

The return's `sprint` field ([converge/SKILL.md:The return](plugins/ok/families/ok-planner/skills/converge/SKILL.md#L149)) says, for each work item and taken improvement, whether it works end to end. It adds lines for the behavior changes, the stories driven, and the checks, and none for the deltas. A delta certification landed shows only as one count among its class's defects in the `fixed` field ([converge/SKILL.md](plugins/ok/families/ok-planner/skills/converge/SKILL.md#L150)). The completion report, the sprint's durable record, carries the return, so it is silent on the deltas too.

At the close, the session runs [review:cmd_certified](plugins/ok/families/ok-planner/scripts/review#L1625-L1640), which checks completion contract item 1 ([plan-sprint/sprint-document.md](plugins/ok/families/ok-planner/skills/plan-sprint/sprint-document.md#L280-L287)): every artifact matches its delta. It prints how many deltas landed, or names each one that did not. The session shows that output to the owner and writes none of it into the report ([plan-sprint/sprint-document.md](plugins/ok/families/ok-planner/skills/plan-sprint/sprint-document.md#L215-L229)). Nothing records which deltas the build missed.

The ruling decides whether certification's return states the deltas' delivery, and in how much detail.
problem.before:
Sprint certification's return never states that the sprint's approved corpus deltas landed, and names a delta only where one did not, so an owner reading the return learns that a delta was delivered only from silence, against [story:certify-completion](.ok-planner/design/stories/certify-completion.md), which promises 'a way to know, when a sprint closes, whether what I approved was delivered, so that "done" means the same thing for every sprint'.

The mechanism. An approved sprint carries two kinds of content: work items, which builders turn into code, and corpus deltas, the final-form text of each concept, story, decision, docspec, or surface intent the sprint changes. Certification's alignment pass compares each delta with its artifact byte for byte ([converge/prompts/sprint-pass.md](plugins/ok/families/ok-planner/skills/converge/prompts/sprint-pass.md#L27)), and a delta that did not land becomes a C3 defect, which the fix loop lands by copying the delta's body into place ([converge/prompts/fix.md](plugins/ok/families/ok-planner/skills/converge/prompts/fix.md#L27)). The return's `sprint` field ([converge/SKILL.md:The return](plugins/ok/families/ok-planner/skills/converge/SKILL.md#L149)) gives one line per work item and taken improvement, saying whether each works end to end, and lines for the docspecs judged, the behavior changes, the stories driven, and the checks. It has no line for deltas. A C3 defect shows only in the `fixed` field, counted by sprint class ([converge/SKILL.md](plugins/ok/families/ok-planner/skills/converge/SKILL.md#L150)), or as stuck. The completion report carries the return, so the report is silent on deltas too.

The state of play. The repository check is built: completion contract item 1 ([plan-sprint/sprint-document.md](plugins/ok/families/ok-planner/skills/plan-sprint/sprint-document.md#L268-L272)) requires every corpus to match every delta, and [decision:final-form-deltas](.ok-planner/design/decisions/final-form-deltas.md) makes that comparison certification's job. The gap is only what the owner reads: a sprint whose approved content is mostly deltas gets a return that speaks for its work items and not for its deltas.

The ruling decides whether certification's return states the deltas' delivery, and in how much detail.

after.text:
Certification's return carries one line for the sprint's corpus deltas: how many it compared, how many had landed at build, how many it landed itself, and how many stuck, naming by artifact each delta it landed and each that stuck.

Rationale: the story asks for a way to know whether what the owner approved was delivered. [decision:final-form-deltas](.ok-planner/design/decisions/final-form-deltas.md) holds that restricting corpus change to the delta gives the sign-off its weight, so the deltas are half of what the owner approves. The return already states delivery for each work item. Option B leaves the deltas to a count the owner sees once at the close, which the completion report never keeps and which does not say which deltas the build missed. Option C keeps that count in the record at the cost of one line, splits it by who landed each delta, and names the deltas worth a look. Option A's line per delta repeats, for every delta that landed, what the count already says. Flip case: if the owner wants each artifact named to check against the sprint they approved, as on a sprint with few deltas, option A gives that at the cost of length.

problem.after:
The review tool falls back to the project root alone when the project's config has any defect, and `/converge` never relays that fallback. A run then reports its hunt and its checks as whole, though they skipped every folder the owner declared.

A project can own folders beside its root, which it lists under `folders` in `.ok-planner/config.json`. [story:project-spans-folders](.ok-planner/design/stories/project-spans-folders.md) promises 'a way to declare every folder my project owns, so that no check the suite runs over my project misses code I own'. `/converge` is the skill that finds and fixes defects. It asks the review tool which files to read and check, and `review files`, `review changed`, and `review checks` all start from the tool's folder list.

To build that list, the tool runs the lint's config check. Where the check finds any defect, such as one entry for a folder since removed, the tool writes a note on stderr, returns no folders, and lets every caller exit 0. The valid folders drop with the stale one. The skill tells the session to relay stderr notes from `issues list` alone, and from `review areas` where no surface intent names a declaring file. So the note never reaches the run's opening line or its return.

`/converge` is the project's skill that finds defects and fixes them. In drive mode and sprint mode, a driver agent uses the product as a user would to get what a story promises, and each story it cannot get becomes a drive defect. The skill then runs fix rounds. In each round, a fixer changes the code, and a verifier reads only that change and accepts or rejects it. Step 6 of each round ([converge/SKILL.md](plugins/ok/families/ok-planner/skills/converge/SKILL.md#L116)) then files one confirm driver for each drive defect the round verified. A confirm driver tries the story again as a user and sends the defect back to the fixers where the story still fails ([converge/prompts/drive.md](plugins/ok/families/ok-planner/skills/converge/prompts/drive.md#L58-L63)).

Step 6 runs `review drives --confirm`, whose [review:confirm_briefs](plugins/ok/families/ok-planner/scripts/review#L1168-L1183) collects only the defects that the current round's verify tasks name. options.text: The review tool decides which defects need a confirm driver. problem:
The session running `/converge` can skip the step that tests a fix by using the product, and no tool catches the skip. The run then reports those defects as fixed, though no one tried them as a user.

`/converge` finds some defects by driving. An agent, the driver, uses the product as a user would and records each failure as a defect. A fixer then changes the code, and a verifier reads only that change. The verifier never runs the product, so each fix round ends with a confirm step: a fresh driver uses the product again and sends the defect back if it still fails.

The skip happens because the session runs the fix loop by hand, from the skill's text. The confirm step applies only to defects a driver found, so the session has to check where each verified defect came from. When the session doesn't check, it goes on to the next round, and no tool stops it. The review tool's confirm command picks only the current round's defects, so once the next round starts, it can no longer pick the skipped ones.

Sessions skipped the step in 2 of the last 8 certification runs, on Oct 4 and Oct 17, and left nine defects unconfirmed. At the owner's word, the session ran the Oct 17 run's eight confirms late. Seven passed. One failed and was fixed again.

The ruling decides how `/converge` makes sure no verified drive defect ends a run without a confirm driver.

recommendation.text:
Take B. B makes the review tool, not the session, decide which defects still need a confirm driver, so the next round or the end of the fix loop recovers a skipped step.

Rationale: sessions skipped a step the skill's text already orders, in two runs, so option C adds more text for the same kind of session to skip. The [rule that every written constraint needs a check that fails on violation](.claude/rules/plumbline-cheatsheet.md) points to the tool, which option B changes. The eight defects this run left unconfirmed have since had their confirm drivers, so no recovery remains to rule on. Flip case: if the owner would rather add no field to the defect record, C is the cheaper ruling, at the cost of relying on the session again.

recommendation.text:
A sprint carries an approval mark that the Approval step writes once the owner approves, and every executor refuses to execute a sprint without it, naming the missing mark. A sprint approved before the mark existed is exempt.

A draft that an executor cannot tell from an approved sprint undoes both, so A leaves the harm in place. The mark follows the precedent of the closing-commit stamp, which records a sprint's lifecycle on the file itself. The refusal sits where the harm happens, at every executor, while C protects only an executor that never sees the draft name, and moves every planning reference at the last step. The flip case: if executors in practice start only from the goal line that Terminal hands over, which a dead session never prints, A's risk is small enough that the template field and the refusals cost more than they save.

The shipped docspec rules let a reference docspec name a class the project keeps internal, and list only that class's members made public by exception. The design documents never say a docspec may do this, so an owner reading them cannot tell whether a reference must list such a member.

A docspec declares one kind of documentation the owner wants kept. A reference docspec's `## Lists` section names the classes of public surface its documentation must list. The surface intent is one document of class rules with named exceptions ([decision:surface-intent-is-one-prose-document](.ok-planner/design/decisions/surface-intent-is-one-prose-document.md)). Such an element reaches a reference only where some `## Lists` names its class. [concept:docspec](.ok-planner/design/concepts/docspec.md) says a reference docspec 'names the classes of public surface the documentation must name in full'. That reads most naturally as classes public by default. Under that reading the element reaches no reference, and nothing notices.

The tooling takes the other reading. The [docspec definition](plugins/ok/families/ok-planner/skills/_shared/artifact-definitions.md#L173) lets `## Lists` name a class 'whose exceptions make a member public', and lists only those members. `/ok-version` fills its plugin-version line from text the project's own copy of the suite wrote, never from the installed ok plugin. Both of its version lines therefore print the same number, and an owner deciding whether to run `/ok` never sees the installed plugin drift from the project.

The project's standalone check refuses any design citation in a script the suite copies into consumer projects, so a story that only such a script realizes has no site that may cite it. The story that the owner can see and overturn every call made in their absence ([story:veto-calls-made-in-my-absence](.ok-planner/design/stories/veto-calls-made-in-my-absence.md)) has no citation in the code, and a search for its annotation finds nothing.

This repository is the suite's source. A design citation is a comment such as `# @story: <slug>` that links code to a design artifact. The build rule puts one at the site that realizes each story ([sprint-document.md step 8](plugins/ok/families/ok-planner/skills/plan-sprint/sprint-document.md#L166-L169)). A payload script is a script true-up, the suite's upgrade pass, copies into every consumer project, such as the task tracker. This story's site is the tracker's calls table, [tasks:calls_table](plugins/ok/families/ok-planner/scripts/tasks#L1305).

[checks/materialized-standalone](checks/materialized-standalone) copies each payload script into a bare git repository and lints it there. That repository declares no citation tags, so any citation fails the lint. The check also refuses, in every markdown payload such as a skill, any citation that resolves in this repository. The check stands because a consumer's lint knows only the tags that consumer declares ([concept:citation-tag](.ok-planner/design/concepts/citation-tag.md)), and a consumer's corpus holds none of the suite's slugs. The sprint that built the calls table planned its citation, and the builder left it out because the check refuses it.

No payload script carries a citation. The true-up core, which runs from the plugin and is never copied, carries about a hundred. True-up already rewrites what it copies: [true-up:render](plugins/ok/families/ok-planner/admin/true-up#L143) rewrites skill prefixes and shared paths and appends the stamp. A missing citation costs only navigation, so no harm the project's review counts as a defect follows.

problem.after:
`review backlog` finds the file names in a defect issue's text with patterns that require a file extension, so it misses a file whose name has none. When such a file is the only one an issue names, the verb reports that the issue names no file, and the `/converge` session acts on that false report.

A `/converge` run in drive, analysis, or defects mode first takes up the intake's defect issues. `review backlog` turns each issue into a report for a merge agent, the agent that checks a report against the code. It lists the files the text names, and takes the first `path:function` as the site. An issue that names no file the run may edit goes under `settled`, with `files: []`, and with each file the run must leave alone under `left_alone`. The session then adds that issue's report itself ([converge/SKILL.md](plugins/ok/families/ok-planner/skills/converge/SKILL.md#L67-L68)). Where `left_alone` is empty, the report's body says the problem names no file of this tree outside the exclude list, which is false here. For a suite-owned file such as `.ok-planner/bin/review`, `left_alone` stays empty too, so the session never routes the issue as one about a file the project does not own. The verb also never takes an extensionless `path:function` as the site.

In a scratch project with a committed `bin/clean` and a defect issue on it, `review backlog` printed `{"reports": [], "settled": [{"issue": "clean-empty-arg", "files": [], "left_alone": {}}]}` and exited 0. A merge agent confirmed the defect in an Oct 17 certification run.

The site is [review:backlog_entry](plugins/ok/families/ok-planner/scripts/review#L979-L993). The entry is [A9](.ok-planner/review/catalog/accept.md#L17): a printed result that a program reads to decide what to do next tells it something that is not so. problem.after:
True-up rewrites a suite file that still carries its stamp without asking git whether the file holds an uncommitted edit, and its consent rule counts that rewrite as safe. An owner who edits such a file and upgrades before committing loses the edit, with no question and no copy. That breaks the promise that an upgrade never costs the owner work they wrote ([story:true-up-project-estate](.ok-planner/design/stories/true-up-project-estate.md)).

True-up is the suite's upgrade pass, which `/ok` runs. It writes suite-owned files into the project, and each one carries a stamp line saying the suite overwrites it. Where a file on disk differs from the version the suite carries, [true-up:materialize_steps](plugins/ok/families/ok-planner/admin/true-up#L4031) queues a rewrite. True-up asks git about a file's state, through [true-up:uncommitted](plugins/ok/families/ok-planner/admin/true-up#L580), only for removals ([true-up:removal_split](plugins/ok/families/ok-planner/admin/true-up#L619)) and for moves into the archive, the folder where true-up keeps files it sets aside.

Before true-up runs, `/ok` asks the owner once where the plan holds a destructive step. A rewrite is destructive only for 'every file but a suite-owned file that still carries its stamp or its fixed content' ([decision:true-up-asks-once-before-destructive-steps](.ok-planner/design/decisions/true-up-asks-once-before-destructive-steps.md)). Lines appended to a stamped file leave the stamp in place, so the plan holds no destructive step and runs with no question. In a scratch project, four uncommitted lines appended to `.claude/rules/plumbline-coding.md` drew 'PLAN: 1 step(s), 0 destructive', and after the run the lines were in no file and not in HEAD.

Every other step that touches work git cannot restore guards it. A removal moves such a file into the archive ([decision:whole-file-ownership](.ok-planner/design/decisions/whole-file-ownership.md)). A retired-layout strip copies it into the archive first and asks ([decision:retired-layout-strips-only-recoverable-files](.ok-planner/design/decisions/retired-layout-strips-only-recoverable-files.md)). A committed edit is safe, since git keeps it.

The ruling decides whether an uncommitted change in a stamped suite file makes its rewrite destructive.
problem.before:
True-up, the suite's upgrade pass, overwrites a suite-owned file that still carries its stamp even where the owner has an uncommitted or staged-only edit in it, with no question and no copy, so the edit is lost. That breaks the promise that upgrading the suite never costs the owner work they wrote ([story:true-up-project-estate](.ok-planner/design/stories/true-up-project-estate.md)).

The mechanism. Where a file on disk differs from the rendering the suite carries, [true-up:materialize_steps](plugins/ok/families/ok-planner/admin/true-up#L4007) queues a rewrite and never asks git whether the difference is committed. The git-state check [true-up:uncommitted](plugins/ok/families/ok-planner/admin/true-up#L570) runs only for removals, through [true-up:removal_split](plugins/ok/families/ok-planner/admin/true-up#L609), and for archive steps. A person who appends lines to a stamped file leaves the stamp in place, so the rule that decides which steps need the owner's consent counts the rewrite as safe: it calls a step destructive where it 'rewrites a file a person edited, which is every file but a suite-owned file that still carries its stamp or its fixed content' ([decision:true-up-asks-once-before-destructive-steps](.ok-planner/design/decisions/true-up-asks-once-before-destructive-steps.md)). The plan then holds no destructive step, and `/ok` runs it with no question. The suite's ownership rule promises that true-up 'never discards uncommitted work' only for 'any other file true-up would remove' ([decision:whole-file-ownership](.ok-planner/design/decisions/whole-file-ownership.md)). In a scratch project, four uncommitted lines appended to `.claude/rules/plumbline-coding.md` drew 'DRIFT: stale: .claude/rules/plumbline-coding.md differs from the carried v26.0.0 rendering' and 'PLAN: 1 step(s), 0 destructive'; after the run the lines were in no file and not in HEAD. An owner who hand-edits a vendored rules file and upgrades before committing loses the edit.

The state of play. A removal of a suite file with an uncommitted change already moves the file into the archive. Stripping a retired layout from a file git cannot restore copies the file into the archive first and counts as destructive ([decision:retired-layout-strips-only-recoverable-files](.ok-planner/design/decisions/retired-layout-strips-only-recoverable-files.md)). A committed edit is safe, since git keeps it, and an unstamped vendored file with the same edit is archived under a destructive step. Only the rewrite of a stamped file with an uncommitted edit has no guard. The story and the two decisions cannot all hold for this file, and no stated rule says which gives way.

The ruling decides whether an uncommitted change in a stamped suite file makes its rewrite destructive.

options.text: A rewrite of a stamped suite file that carries an uncommitted or staged-only change counts as destructive: true-up copies the working file into the archive first, and the plan asks the owner once; cost: a question on an upgrade where the owner edited a file whose stamp says not to, and a git-state check on every stale file.

options.label: B
options.text: The suite states that a stamped file's uncommitted edits are discarded on rewrite, and the story narrows the work it protects to files the owner owns; cost: an owner who edits a stamped file loses the edit with no notice.

options.label: C
options.text: True-up rewrites with no question but copies the uncommitted working file into the archive first and names it in its report; cost: the archive grows with copies the owner may not want, and an archive move without consent departs from the rule that every archive move is destructive.

options.label: D
options.text: True-up rewrites with no question and names each discarded uncommitted change by path in its report; cost: the edit is still lost, only named.

problem:
True-up rewrites a suite file that still carries its stamp without asking git whether the file holds an uncommitted edit, and its consent rule counts that rewrite as safe. An owner who edits such a file and upgrades before committing loses the edit, with no question and no copy. That breaks the promise that an upgrade never costs the owner work they wrote ([story:true-up-project-estate](.ok-planner/design/stories/true-up-project-estate.md)).

True-up is the suite's upgrade pass, which `/ok` runs. It writes suite-owned files into the project, and each one carries a stamp line saying the suite overwrites it. Where a file on disk differs from the version the suite carries, [true-up:materialize_steps](plugins/ok/families/ok-planner/admin/true-up#L4031) queues a rewrite. True-up asks git about a file's state, through [true-up:uncommitted](plugins/ok/families/ok-planner/admin/true-up#L580), only for removals ([true-up:removal_split](plugins/ok/families/ok-planner/admin/true-up#L619)) and for moves into the archive, the folder where true-up keeps files it sets aside.

Before true-up runs, `/ok` asks the owner once where the plan holds a destructive step. A rewrite is destructive only for 'every file but a suite-owned file that still carries its stamp or its fixed content' ([decision:true-up-asks-once-before-destructive-steps](.ok-planner/design/decisions/true-up-asks-once-before-destructive-steps.md)). Lines appended to a stamped file leave the stamp in place, so the plan holds no destructive step and runs with no question. In a scratch project, four uncommitted lines appended to `.claude/rules/plumbline-coding.md` drew 'PLAN: 1 step(s), 0 destructive', and after the run the lines were in no file and not in HEAD.

Every other step that touches work git cannot restore guards it. A removal moves such a file into the archive ([decision:whole-file-ownership](.ok-planner/design/decisions/whole-file-ownership.md)). A retired-layout strip copies it into the archive first and asks ([decision:retired-layout-strips-only-recoverable-files](.ok-planner/design/decisions/retired-layout-strips-only-recoverable-files.md)). A committed edit is safe, since git keeps it.

The ruling decides whether an uncommitted change in a stamped suite file makes its rewrite destructive.

recommendation.text:
Count a rewrite of a stamped suite file that carries an uncommitted or staged-only change as destructive. True-up copies the working file into the archive before it rewrites it, the plan marks the step destructive, and the owner's one consent covers it. A rewrite of a stamped file whose difference git holds in a commit stays a rewrite with no question.

Rationale: the story promises that an upgrade never costs the owner work they wrote, and the suite already keeps that promise for every other step that touches work git cannot restore: a removal archives such a file, and a retired-layout strip copies it into the archive first and asks. The consent rule uses the stamp to tell an untouched suite file from an edited one, and an appended edit leaves the stamp in place, so the stamp test misses the case the rule means to catch. A applies the suite's existing recoverability test to the one step that lacks it. B gives up the story for a file the owner can change with any editor. C keeps the text but moves a file into the archive without the consent the suite asks for every other archive move. D only reports the loss. The flip case: if owners in practice never hand-edit stamped files, and the uncommitted differences true-up meets are its own earlier output the owner has not yet committed, the question is noise, and D's report line would serve the owner as well at less cost.

title: True-up rewrites stamped suite files without checking git for uncommitted edits

options.label: A
options.text: Give `review prompt` a `--block <TOKEN>` option, or a new verb, that writes a block-defined prompt from its block source with its transclusions resolved and its placeholders filled, and have step 3 of the sprint boilerplate name that command.

problem:
Step 3 of the sprint execution boilerplate tells each sprint session to write the sprint build prompt from a block, and `review prompt` reads only converge prompt templates, so every session assembles the build prompt by hand.

**Mechanism.** [`plugins/ok/families/ok-planner/skills/plan-sprint/sprint-document.md`](plugins/ok/families/ok-planner/skills/plan-sprint/sprint-document.md#L118), step 3 of "How to execute this sprint", says to "write `{{SPRINT-BUILD-PROMPT}}` from [`.claude/skills/_sprint/shared.md`](.claude/skills/_sprint/shared.md), its transclusions resolved and `[SPRINT PATH]` filled". The block lives in the block source [`skills/_sprint/shared.md`](plugins/ok/families/ok-planner/skills/_sprint/shared.md). `review prompt` ([`scripts/review`](plugins/ok/families/ok-planner/scripts/review), [`cmd_prompt`](plugins/ok/families/ok-planner/scripts/review#L546)) takes only `--name`, `--out`, `--sprint`, and `--base`, and reads templates only from `.claude/skills/converge/prompts/`, so `review prompt --name build --out <path>` refuses with "cannot read prompt template .../.claude/skills/converge/prompts/build.md". The tool already parses block sources for transclusions ([`block_sources`](plugins/ok/families/ok-planner/scripts/review#L503)), but no verb writes a block as a prompt.

**Harm.** Each sprint session assembles the prompt with a scratch script, and a hand assembly can drift from the block it copies.

**Evidence.** linescout-inl `platform/`, ok-planner v28.0.0, 2026-10-23: `review prompt --help` lists no option for a block. The project first met the gap under v25.3.0, when the session of the 2026-10-17 console front proxy sprint built its prompt with a scratch script reusing the tool's block parsing.
reason: No accept-list entry covers this defect claim. The code stands as filed (plugins/ok/families/ok-planner/scripts/review:cmd_prompt reads only converge templates), but a session that assembles the build prompt by hand follows the designed path: decision single-source-transclusion says "The running model replaces each token when it assembles a dispatch", and the boilerplate step names no tool verb, so no A8 rule decides the fix and no A3 or A9 harm follows; drift in a hand assembly is a risk with no trigger on a correctly configured system. Adding a block-writing verb is a tooling feature the owner can file as a judgment issue.
title: The review tool has no way to write the sprint build prompt the sprint boilerplate tells every session to write

problem.after:
Each agent gets its role's shared prompt from the output of its `tasks claim` call, and that output comes after text that differs between agents. So the prompt cache cannot share it, and each agent pays to cache about 2,000 tokens an earlier agent already cached.

The task tracker starts every agent of one profile from one identical first message, so those agents share one cached prefix, as [decision:no-execution-engine](.ok-planner/design/decisions/no-execution-engine.md) says. A profile is the agent definition that fixes an agent's model and first message. A role is a kind of task, such as build, with one prompt file per run. The agent's first act is `tasks claim`, and the claim's output joins the agent's next request. A prompt cache matches a request from its start and stops at the first difference.

[tasks:cmd_claim](plugins/ok/families/ok-planner/scripts/tasks#L875-L883) prints the task's own lines first, then the role prompt. Printing the prompt first would not help. The claim's output follows the agent's own tool call in the request. The API gives each call a fresh id, and the model words each call's command and description its own way. So two agents' requests differ before the claim's output begins. Agents that start together also gain nothing until the first one has written the cache.

One sprint on 2026-10-22 ran 20 build tasks under one build prompt of about 8.7 KB. Other runs start agents the same way. No accept-list entry names this cost.

The ruling decides whether the role prompt moves to where agents share it from the cache, and how.

reason: The owner accepted triage's recommendation by silence at the fifth intake drain sprint's planning: leave the order tasks claim prints in, and accept one cache write of the role prompt per agent. Reordering saves nothing while each agent's claim call differs, and a profile per role cannot hold a prompt a run fills in.

recommendation.text:
Leave the order that `tasks claim` prints in, and accept one cache write of the role prompt per agent.

Rationale: [decision:no-execution-engine](.ok-planner/design/decisions/no-execution-engine.md) promises one cached prefix per profile, and the identical first message already keeps that promise. Flip case: if a run's bill shows the role prompt's cache writes as a material share of its cost, as with many short agents whose working context is small, B earns its extra profiles; if the harness makes the claim call identical across agents, A becomes the cheap fix.

problem.after:
/plan-tests tells its runtime planner to end some scenario ids with an upper-case harm code, and the plan's assembly check refuses any id that is not lower case. The skill's only remedy reruns the whole planner, so one upper-case letter cost a project a full planning pass and the owner's review of its scenarios.

/plan-tests plans a test sprint, one test per scenario. Planner agents, one per story and one for runtime parts, file the scenarios, and the task tracker records any id. [The runtime prompt](plugins/ok/families/ok-planner/skills/plan-tests/core.md#L213-L214) names a new scenario `runtime--<part>--<class>`, "with the harm's entry where one part and class carry two harms". [tests plan](plugins/ok/families/ok-planner/scripts/tests#L602-L604) then refuses an id that is not lower-case letters, digits, and hyphens. [Step 7](plugins/ok/families/ok-planner/skills/plan-tests/SKILL.md#L58) answers a refusal by refiling the planner, whose new items replace the old ones under [step 5](plugins/ok/families/ok-planner/skills/plan-tests/SKILL.md#L45). No step tells the session to fix an item.

On the linescout platform project, at ok-planner v28.0.0, the runtime planner filed `runtime--query-engine--dependency-down--A7`, the prompt's own form. 437 other ids passed. The refile cost about 100,000 tokens and replaced all 52 runtime scenarios the owner had reviewed.

Under any ruling, the prompt must name a form the check accepts. The ruling decides where else the id's shape is checked, and what remedy the skill gives a mechanical failure.

recommendation.text:
The runtime naming rule takes a lower-case harm suffix, such as `--a7`, so the prompt names only ids the check accepts. The check stays at assembly, and /plan-tests gains a mechanical repair step: the session renames a refused id in place, and refiles a planner only for a failure that needs its judgment. Rule this together with plan-tests-fixes-a-finding-by-rebuilding-the-planner, whose mechanical edit step covers this rename.

Rationale: the naming rule caused the failure, so fixing it removes the case at its source, and the repair step covers the next slip for a few tokens. Neither touches the tracker, which [decision:no-execution-engine](.ok-planner/design/decisions/no-execution-engine.md) keeps from judging what it records, as option A would have it do. A planner-side check catches a slip in the planner's own turn, but it adds a verb and a step to every planner prompt for a failure the fixed rule makes rare. The flip case: if planners still file ids the check refuses after the rule is fixed, add the planner-side check so each planner checks its own items before it closes.

problem.after:
/plan-tests has no way to change one scenario: each fix reruns the planner that wrote it, which rebuilds all its scenarios. A small fix costs a full planning pass, and scenarios the owner reviewed come back rewritten, some under new ids.

One /plan-tests planner agent per story, plus one runtime planner, files scenarios, the outcomes a test must check, as items in a task run. [Step 5](plugins/ok/families/ok-planner/skills/plan-tests/SKILL.md#L45) says a rerun planner's items "replace the earlier task's". [Step 7](plugins/ok/families/ok-planner/skills/plan-tests/SKILL.md#L58) answers an assembly failure by rerunning the planner, and [step 9](plugins/ok/families/ok-planner/skills/plan-tests/SKILL.md#L66) and [step 10](plugins/ok/families/ok-planner/skills/plan-tests/SKILL.md#L70) answer a review finding and an owner's change the same way. [The planner prompts](plugins/ok/families/ok-planner/skills/plan-tests/core.md) never read the run's earlier items, so a rerun planner sees a finding only in its brief and files a new set. No step lets the session edit a planner's items, and no item state marks a scenario dropped.

On the linescout platform project, at ok-planner v28.0.0, a rerun over one malformed id rewrote all 52 runtime scenarios. The plan review then raised 44 findings across about 38 planners: fold extra scenarios, drop a few, and correct one outcome's wording. Fixing them as the skill says costs about 4 million tokens.

The ruling decides how /plan-tests applies a fix to one planner's scenarios.

recommendation.text:
The session applies each finding whose fix is mechanical, a rename, a drop, a fold, or a wording fix, by editing the planner's items in place, and a dropped item leaves the plan. A finding that needs a planner's judgment goes back as a revision refile: the planner reads its earlier items and the finding, and changes only what the finding names. The same two paths serve an assembly failure and an owner's change at approval. Rule this together with plan-tests-rejects-a-malformed-scenario-id-only-at-assembly, whose rename repair is one case of the edit step.

Neither path asks the tracker to judge, so [decision:no-execution-engine](.ok-planner/design/decisions/no-execution-engine.md) holds. The edit step alone still rebuilds a whole planner for one judgment finding, and the revision refile alone spends a planner run on a rename. The flip case: if the owner wants one new mechanism, take the edit step alone, since mechanical findings carry most of the cost.

problem.after:
/plan-tests files one review task for the whole test plan, so one agent reads the whole plan at once. On a large plan that agent reads more than one pass can check closely, and its findings come back as one list that sends most planners back.

/plan-tests plans a test sprint: one planner agent per story and one runtime planner each record scenarios, the outcomes a test must check. [Step 9](plugins/ok/families/ok-planner/skills/plan-tests/SKILL.md#L66) then files one review task under the [review prompt](plugins/ok/families/ok-planner/skills/plan-tests/core.md#L336-L380), and refiles, or reruns, the planner each finding names. Most of that prompt's checks read one planner's scenarios alone: each scenario names a story's way, states an outcome, and reaches the code through a public entry point. One check spans the plan: every owner answer holds. Planning is split per story; the review is not. The corpus says nothing about how the review is split.

On the linescout platform project, at ok-planner v28.0.0, the plan held 485 scenarios from 108 planners. The one reviewer used about 538,000 tokens and returned 44 findings touching about 38 planners. 26 of the findings flagged a planner that split one story way into several scenarios, a check that reads one planner's scenarios alone. The issue on that cap, plan-tests-caps-each-story-way-at-one-scenario-per-program, changes what any split review checks, so the two rule together.

The ruling decides how /plan-tests splits the review of a test plan.

problem.after:
The task tracker can add and change the items agents file, but cannot remove one. An item filed by mistake stays in every later read, and the only sanctioned way to remove it is to rerun the agent that filed it.

The task tracker is the durable record of one run of agent work: the tasks an orchestrator files, and the items agents file into named pools as they work. [concept:task-tracker](.ok-planner/design/concepts/task-tracker.md) says a later reader learns what each task produced from the record alone. Its [item verbs](plugins/ok/families/ok-planner/scripts/tasks#L1487-L1512) are add, list, count, and set; set changes an item's state, note, key, and fields, and cannot remove the item or detach it from its task. The /plan-tests assembler, which builds a test plan from the planners' items, [reads every item in a pool](plugins/ok/families/ok-planner/scripts/tests#L412-L413) whatever its state, and keeps each item of a planner's latest finished task. [The estate guide](plugins/ok/families/ok-planner/scripts/ok-planner-CLAUDE.md#L498) says: "Never hand-edit a run file; the tracker's verbs are the only writers."

On the linescout platform project, at ok-planner v28.0.0, four planners filed five items that retire scenarios on a first test plan, which has nothing to retire, and the assembler refused all five. Removing them by the tracker's verbs meant rerunning the four planners, about 280,000 tokens. The owner instead approved deleting the run-file lines by hand and rebuilding the index, against the rule above.

The ruling decides how an orchestrator removes an item from a run.

problem.after:
`/converge`'s fix loop retries a defect still marked in progress only when its fix task fails. When a fixer closes its task as done but leaves its defect in progress, no verifier checks the defect, nothing reports it, and the run ends with the defect unfixed.

`/converge` lists the defects a run found. Each round, the fix loop marks every `open` defect `fixing` and files fix tasks. Each fixer sets its defect `fixed`, `declined`, or `duplicate`, and verifiers check only those. The loop ends when no defect stands `open`. An owner-list agent then files each defect the run left into the issue intake. A fix task that closes `partial`, `blocked`, or `disputed` gets one retry, and then its `fixing` defects return to `open`. No step covers a `done` close, and the task tracker allows one whatever its defects' states.

An agent testing the loop closed a fix task `done` without setting its defect. The defect stayed `fixing`, no verifier ran, and the loop's end check passed.

problem.after:
None of `/plan-docs`'s edit rules fires when documentation departs from its docspec's reader or coverage. An owner who changes whom a kind of documentation is for, or what it covers, never sees the documentation change.

A docspec is the owner's order for one kind of documentation: where it lives, its reader (`## Reader`), what it covers (`## Covers`), and its shape. `/plan-docs` plans a documentation sprint for each docspec whose text or references changed since its stamp, the commit its documentation was last checked at. The writer edits a file only where one of six rules fires: a false claim, a missing public element, a shown internal element, a sprint that changed what a user can do, a departure from the shape or layout, or a claim no one can settle. Every other sentence stays as written. problem.after:
The project allows documentation comments only in the files a docspec names, but the lint reads a Python docstring as a string, not a comment, so a docstring in any Python file passes the lint.

A docspec is the owner's declaration of one kind of documentation the project keeps. A docspec whose `## Where` opens with `in code:` names the files that may carry documentation comments. The rule in [.claude/rules/plumbline-cheatsheet.md](.claude/rules/plumbline-cheatsheet.md) says documentation comments are written "only in the files an in-code docspec covers", and its Mechanical Checks rule says "Every written constraint needs a check that fails on violation". [decision:comments-forbidden-by-default](.ok-planner/design/decisions/comments-forbidden-by-default.md) allows documentation comments only "in the files an in-code docspec covers". The lint's `comment-hygiene` check enforces this for TypeScript and Go: a `/** ... */` comment outside the named files fails. The lint's Python grammar declares only `#` comments, and its string reader consumes a `"""..."""` docstring before the comment check sees it.

In a scratch project, a docspec named `src/tool.py` and `src/tool.ts`. A `/** Help. */` comment in `src/other.ts` exited 2. A `"""Help."""` docstring on `def helper():` in `src/other.py` exited 0. A `#` prose comment in the same Python file exited 2, so the check runs on Python. The cheatsheet names one compliant form: the lint refuses the docstring. The project's own Python scripts carry docstrings, such as [scripts/tasks:instructions](plugins/ok/families/ok-planner/scripts/tasks#L578), which the cheatsheet says to leave as they stand.

problem.after:
The text form of `issues show` prints each person's message with its current text alone. It drops the earlier text and the edited and withdrawn marks the intake keeps. A reader sees a reply to a question the output no longer shows. `/triage-issues`'s respond agent reads the same output, so it cannot tell an edited question from a new one, or skip a withdrawn one.

A person may edit or withdraw their own message after triage answers it. The intake then keeps the earlier text under `earlier` and stamps `edited` or `withdrawn`. [decision:owner-messages-can-change](.ok-planner/design/decisions/owner-messages-can-change.md) commits to this: "A message an answer already followed keeps its earlier text beside the change", so each reply stays readable against what it answered. [decision:triage-answers-owner-messages](.ok-planner/design/decisions/triage-answers-owner-messages.md) says "a message its author withdraws needs no answer". The respond prompt's Judge step tells its agent to answer what changed in an edited message and to act on nothing a withdrawn one says. Its Read step has the agent read the text form of `issues show <id>`, not `--json`. An edit of an answered message also sets `seen` back to null, so a message edited and then withdrawn prints as `not yet seen`.

In a scratch project, triage answered two comments. Their author edited one, and edited and then removed the other on the dashboard. `issues show` printed both as plain current text marked `not yet seen`. `issues show --json` and the dashboard both carried `earlier`, `edited`, and `withdrawn`. One fix, to the text output or to the prompt's read, closes both sites.

problem.after:
`docs complete`, the command that says whether a documentation run is done, never asks whether any claim was checked. A run that skips its checks still prints `DOCS COMPLETE`, and the owner then records unchecked documentation as current.

A documentation sprint writes a project's documentation. Writers edit the files, and a style pass reads each changed file. Then checkers, who wrote none of it, check each claim until it holds or is cut, per [decision:documentation-claims-checked-until-they-hold](.ok-planner/design/decisions/documentation-claims-checked-until-they-hold.md) and [decision:documentation-claim-ledger](.ok-planner/design/decisions/documentation-claim-ledger.md). That session moves it to `.ok-planner/history/discoveries/` with `git mv` and leaves the move uncommitted.

Step 2 lists the sprint file, its sidecar, the release boundaries, the intake files, and the archived sketches, but not the discovery. The archive step names the sprint's change, the moved sprint files, the run's ledger, and the intake, but neither the discovery nor the sketches. An executor that reads "the sprint's change" as the build's work commits neither.

problem.after:
`/converge` starts the product under one fixed run name, `drive`, and after a failed start it stops whatever run holds that name. When a second run's start fails because a first run holds the name, the second run takes down the first run's live product.

A `/converge` drive tests the project's stories against the running product, its stack. The reference stack tool, `.ok-planner/bin/stack`, starts each stack as a run under a name. The drive's start line is `stack up --name drive`, and its stop line is `stack down --name drive`. `stack up` refuses where a live run already holds the name. After a failed start, drive step 2 runs the stop line to take down "what the failed start left". The stack helpers document says no run then holds the name. That holds only where the failed start opened the run. A refused start opened nothing.

In a scratch-project test, a first run started and served. A second run's start was refused because the first held the name. The second run's stop line then printed `took down: run-cfc94a3e1f1b (WEB_PORT=44856; 1 container(s), ...)`, and the first run's server was gone.

The site is [converge/SKILL.md:In drive mode step 2](plugins/ok/families/ok-planner/skills/converge/SKILL.md#L79), with the stop line in [ADMINISTRATION.md:Stack declaration](plugins/ok/families/ok-planner/admin/ADMINISTRATION.md#L225) and [stack-helpers.md](plugins/ok/families/ok-planner/docs/stack-helpers.md#L438-L444). Accept-list entry A2 covers it: cleanup reaches something it did not create. The trigger is a second verification run in the same checkout whose `stack up --name drive` is refused because a live run holds the name. Step 2 reads "Where the start fails, the drive ends: say so, with the output tail, file and drain step 4's `stack-stop` task, which takes down what the failed start left". ADMINISTRATION.md:225 writes the stop line `.ok-planner/bin/stack down --name drive; s=$?; .ok-planner/bin/stack cleanup; exit $s`. stack-helpers.md:443 reads "after a failed start no run holds the name, and `down --name` exits 0". problem.after:
The port registry asks docker which ports its containers publish and sets no time limit on the call. When docker's daemon hangs instead of refusing, every new `stack up` and `ports lease` stalls with no bound and no message.

The port registry, `.ok-planner/bin/ports`, leases host ports to verification runs. Its `lease` verb counts a port as taken when a docker container publishes it. It lists them through the docker sweep, a helper that runs `docker ps -a -q` and `docker container inspect`. The reference stack tool's `stack up` leases through the registry, and `/converge`'s drive runs `stack up` unattended. The registry's help says lease skips the docker check where docker's daemon does not answer. The code skips the check only when docker exits with an error. A daemon that accepts the connection and never answers holds the call forever.

During one drive, docker's daemon hung for a few minutes. `stack up --name drive` waited over 2.5 minutes on its child `docker ps -a -q` until killed. A separate `ports lease` never returned. Once docker answered, a lease returned at once.

problem.after:
`docs window` watches a listed class's declaring files only where the class's name matches a line in the surface intent, and it says nothing about a class that matches none. A new public member of that class then leaves the docspec marked current, and the owner running `/plan-docs` never learns that the names differ.

A docspec is the owner's order for one kind of documentation. A reference docspec's `## Lists` names the classes of public surface it lists in full, "in the surface intent's terms". The surface intent is the owner's declaration of the public surface. Its last section names, for each class, the files that declare the class's members. `/plan-docs` runs `docs window` to learn which docspecs fall behind the product. The tool reaches a reference docspec when the surface intent changes, or when a file declaring a listed class changes.

The tool lowercases each class name and collapses its spaces. It keeps each declaring line whose name then equals a `## Lists` bullet, and returns only that line's paths. No caller learns which listed class matched nothing.

A driver, an agent that uses the product as a user would, listed two classes, one with no declaring line, then added a member of that class. `docs window` printed `status: current` with no note. Listing `The CLI verbs` against a declaring line `CLI verbs` did the same, and renaming the line to match reached the docspec.

Site: [docs:declaring_paths](plugins/ok/families/ok-planner/scripts/docs#L209-L219), with [docs:window_entry](plugins/ok/families/ok-planner/scripts/docs#L290-L330). Entry: A3, an owner's mistake made through `/plan-docs` (a class named in `## Lists` that no declaring line names) gives a wrong result and no message that tells the owner what they did wrong. Trigger: a reference docspec whose `## Lists` names a class with no declaring line of the same normalized name. Evidence: [docs:216-218](plugins/ok/families/ok-planner/scripts/docs#L216-L218) `if found and class_name(found.group(1)) in wanted: paths.extend(QUOTED.findall(found.group(2)))`; [docs:318](plugins/ok/families/ok-planner/scripts/docs#L318) `for ref in declaring_paths(root, spec["lists"]):` returns paths only, so no caller learns which listed class matched nothing.

A docspec is the owner's order for one kind of documentation. A reference docspec's `## Lists` names the classes of public surface it lists in full, "in the surface intent's terms". The surface intent is the owner's declaration of the public surface; its last section names, for each class, the files that declare the class's members. `/plan-docs` runs `docs window` to learn which docspecs fall behind the product. The tool puts a reference docspec in the window when the surface intent changes or when a file it names as declaring a listed class changes.

The tool keeps only the declaring lines whose normalized class name equals a `## Lists` bullet, and it skips a listed class that matches none. A driver listed two classes, one with no declaring line, then added a member of that class: `docs window` printed `status: current` with no note. Listing `The CLI verbs` against a declaring line `CLI verbs` did the same, and renaming the line to match opened the window.

problem.after:
`/plan-tests` sorts each old fixture in a batch apart from the tests that read it, and no later step checks that sort against the tests the plan keeps. A fixture a kept test needs can be deleted, and a fixture no kept test needs can stay.

A test sprint is the one run that writes and deletes tests. On a project's first one, `/plan-tests` sorts the existing tests, the legacy suite, with no question per test. A test that checks a planned scenario, one way a story's promise is met, is adopted and stays. Under [decision:legacy-suites-sorted-automatically](.ok-planner/design/decisions/legacy-suites-sorted-automatically.md), the run deletes "a fixture or a data file no kept test uses".

The session files one sort task per ten files, in path order, and the sort agents run side by side. The sort rules mark a fixture `support` only where "an adopted test uses" it, but each agent sees only its own batch. The plan check confirms that a `support` entry names a planned scenario, and never that a kept test reads the file.

A needed fixture sorted `delete` is removed, and its adopted test fails. The fix agents may not touch a fixture, so they cannot make that test pass, and the test is lost. An unused fixture sorted `support` counts as claimed, so the cleanup step never deletes it.
