problem.after:
When the project's test command runs a whole file rather than one named test, `/plan-tests` sorts each legacy test file as one unit. Orphan and duplicate tests inside a kept file then survive the test sprint that should delete them.

A test sprint is the one run that writes and deletes tests. On its first run, `/plan-tests` sorts the tests already in the project, the legacy suite, against scenarios. A scenario is one way a story's promise is met. [decision:legacy-suites-sorted-automatically](.ok-planner/design/decisions/legacy-suites-sorted-automatically.md) sorts "every test no scenario claims". It deletes each orphan, "A test that checks the code against itself, or a behavior no story or rule names". Where two legacy tests check one scenario, "the first is adopted and the second deleted as a duplicate". The project declares its test command as `testing.run`, holding `{name}` only "where the runner needs it" ([decision:scenario-list-decided-once](.ok-planner/design/decisions/scenario-list-decided-once.md)).

The sort prompt sorts by test name only where `testing.run` holds `{name}`, and by file otherwise. The plan locates a test with no name by its bare path, and the plan check refuses two scenarios that share one locator.

A driver, an agent that uses the product as a user would, traced the sort under a command such as `npx jest {path}`. A kept file keeps its orphan tests, with the private imports that block a later code removal. In a file whose tests check two scenarios, the second scenario gets a new test, and its legacy tests stay.

problem.after:
A test sprint's close asks the owner to veto any old test it deleted or ported, but its one step that acts on a veto handles only calls. A vetoed deletion or port is neither restored nor filed as an issue, and the archive commit carries it as if the owner accepted it.

A test sprint is the one run that writes and deletes tests. On a project's first one, the run deletes each old test that guards no promise. It ports each test of a rule on the code's shape: it rewrites the test as a project check, a program the review loop runs, and deletes the test. [decision:legacy-suites-sorted-automatically](.ok-planner/design/decisions/legacy-suites-sorted-automatically.md) says "The completion report lists each deletion and each port for the owner's veto." [story:veto-calls-made-in-my-absence](.ok-planner/design/stories/veto-calls-made-in-my-absence.md) promises the owner a way to see each call "so that I can overturn one I disagree with". A call is a judgment an agent recorded without the owner.

The close's last step shows the deletions and ports beside the calls. It then files one issue "for each vetoed call" and offers the archive. The report tool lists deletions and ports apart from the calls. By then `tests complete` has ended the sprint, so the lint refuses an edit that restores a test. The issue the step files for a vetoed call is the shape the rule leaves for it.

The intake tool, `.ok-planner/bin/issues`, starts tracking what a person has read at that person's first read, never at their first comment or ruling. A person who writes first never sees the answers that land before their first read, the reply to their own question included.

problem.after:
A documentation sprint's closing steps file one issue for each call the owner vetoes, but never record the owner's words as its ruling. If the owner then says nothing, the next planning session can adopt a recommendation that keeps the vetoed call.

`/plan-docs` writes a documentation sprint, a plan that agents carry out to write the project's documentation. A call is a judgment an agent made without the owner, and the owner may veto any call at the documentation sprint's close. [story:veto-calls-made-in-my-absence](.ok-planner/design/stories/veto-calls-made-in-my-absence.md) promises the owner a way to overturn such a call.

The closes of a `/plan-sprint` sprint and of a `/converge` run also record the owner's words with `issues rule <id> --text -`, as [decision:converge-close-takes-vetoes](.ok-planner/design/decisions/converge-close-takes-vetoes.md) says. Only a ruled issue reaches the next `/plan-sprint` as the owner's decision. On an unruled issue, triage writes its own recommended ruling, and the owner's silence accepts it. The test sprint's close has the same gap, filed apart as test-sprint-veto-filed-without-ruling.

problem.after:
The `/ok-version` skill reports the ok plugin version installed on the machine, while its story promises the version that governs the running session. After a plugin update and before a reload, the two differ, and the owner reads a version the session has not loaded.

The ok suite ships as a Claude Code plugin. `/ok`, the suite's administration command, copies files from the plugin into the project, its vendored layer, and stamps each copy with the plugin's version. Under [decision:per-project-pinning](.ok-planner/design/decisions/per-project-pinning.md), every session runs the vendored layer and only `/ok` runs from the plugin; the decision calls the gap between the vendored stamp and the plugin "the useful signal". `/ok` updates the plugin first and copies from the new install.

[story:see-governing-versions](.ok-planner/design/stories/see-governing-versions.md) reads: "I want a way to see which plugin version governs my current session beside the version this project's vendored layer carries, so that version drift is visible."

The skill's [step 1](plugins/ok/families/ok-planner/skills/ok-version/SKILL.md#L12-L14) reads the installed version from `claude plugin list --json`. The skill runs from the vendored layer, so it has no direct way to learn which version the session loaded. Its conduct line still reports the conduct that governs the session, so one report mixes an installed value with session values.

The ruling decides which plugin version the story promises to show: the one the session loaded, or the one installed for the next `/ok` run.

The `/ok-version` skill reports the ok plugin version installed on the machine, while its story promises the version that governs the running session. After a plugin update and before a reload, the two differ, and the owner reads a version the session has not loaded.

The ok suite ships as a Claude Code plugin. `/ok`, the suite's administration command, updates the plugin, then copies files from it into the project and stamps each copy with the plugin's version. These copies are the project's vendored layer. Under [decision:per-project-pinning](.ok-planner/design/decisions/per-project-pinning.md), every session runs the vendored layer, and only `/ok` runs from the plugin. The decision calls the gap between the vendored stamp and the plugin "the useful signal".

[story:see-governing-versions](.ok-planner/design/stories/see-governing-versions.md) reads: "I want a way to see which plugin version governs my current session beside the version this project's vendored layer carries, so that version drift is visible."

The skill's [step 1](plugins/ok/families/ok-planner/skills/ok-version/SKILL.md#L12-L14) reads the installed version from `claude plugin list --json`. The skill runs from the vendored layer, so it has no direct way to learn which version the session loaded. Its conduct line reports the session's conduct, so one report mixes an installed value with a session value.

The ruling decides which plugin version the story promises to show: the one the session loaded, or the one installed for the next `/ok` run.

problem.after:
The hook that lints each agent edit reads only a tool call's `file_path` input, so an edit made through Bash or the notebook editor lands unchecked. A Read of an untracked file that holds a comment, though, blocks the agent.

The lint checks a file for residue, such as prose comments. True-up, the step that installs the suite into a project, wires the hook to run after every tool call. The hook [reads only the input's `file_path`](plugins/ok/families/ok-planner/scripts/hooks/post-edit.js#L41-L42) and passes when the input has none. A Bash call names no file, and NotebookEdit names its file in `notebook_path`. The lint also has [no grammar for `.ipynb` files](plugins/ok/families/ok-planner/scripts/plumbline#L64-L91). Read carries `file_path` too, so the hook lints each file Read opens. Claude Code's auto mode tells agents they may make small edits through Bash.

[story:edit-time-lint-enforcement](.ok-planner/design/stories/edit-time-lint-enforcement.md) promises "every agent edit checked against the lint checks my project turned on as it lands". [decision:edit-hook-blocks-in-turn](.ok-planner/design/decisions/edit-hook-blocks-in-turn.md) scopes the hook to the edited file's changed lines, and does not say which tools count as edits. The [cheatsheet](plugins/ok/families/ok-planner/docs/plumbline-cheatsheet.md#L161) says the hook "does nothing for a Bash call". The review loop lints changed files later.

A driver fed the wired hook Claude Code tool payloads. The hook checked Edit, Write, and MultiEdit. A Bash call that wrote a prose comment passed, and so did a NotebookEdit whose cell held one. A Read of an untracked file that holds a comment blocked.

The ruling decides whether the edit-time check covers edits made through Bash and notebooks.

problem.after:
/plan-docs plans only from the docspecs, the owner's documentation orders, that exist now. When a sprint retires a docspec or points it at new files, the old files stay. No later run drops or checks them, so readers find documentation of an older product.

Each docspec's `## Where` section names its files, and only a documentation sprint writes documentation. /plan-docs first runs [docs window](plugins/ok/families/ok-planner/scripts/docs#L333-L340), which lists only the docspecs that exist. [The planner](plugins/ok/families/ok-planner/skills/plan-docs/core.md#L110-L120) reads only the files under each current `## Where`.

An agent testing the product retired a docspec in a scratch project after an earlier run had written its guide. `docs window` then printed "the project declares no documentation", and [/plan-docs](plugins/ok/families/ok-planner/skills/plan-docs/SKILL.md#L18) stops there. The guide and its run record stayed tracked. A sprint that moves a `## Where` leaves the old files the same way.

[story:keep-documentation-current](.ok-planner/design/stories/keep-documentation-current.md) promises a way to bring "every document my project keeps" up to date. One reading covers the files a retired docspec left. The other covers only what a standing docspec declares, and leaves those files to the retiring sprint, whose builders [decision:documentation-sprints-write-the-documentation](.ok-planner/design/decisions/documentation-sprints-write-the-documentation.md) bars from writing documentation.

The ruling decides who answers for documentation a docspec no longer covers.

problem.after:
The decision behind `/ok`'s one consent question says nothing about a second plan that destroys files, so the skill picks an answer of its own. When the owner declines that second plan, the project's configuration keeps an answer that the files built from it do not show.

`/ok` brings a project's copy of the suite up to the current version. It shows the owner the whole plan and asks once: go ahead with all of it, or abort. A step is destructive where it deletes or archives a file, or rewrites a file a person edited. [decision:true-up-asks-once-before-destructive-steps](.ok-planner/design/decisions/true-up-asks-once-before-destructive-steps.md) says that on abort `/ok` writes nothing and the project stays on the version its stamps record.

After the first plan runs, `/ok` asks the input questions, such as which lint checks to turn off, applies the answers, and plans again. The second plan turns destructive in two cases: an answer unblocks a destructive step, or an answer changes a file the first plan wrote, so the second plan must archive and rewrite that file.

[Step 5.4 of /ok](plugins/ok/skills/ok/SKILL.md#L72) answers a declined second plan by writing nothing more, reporting `trued up; plan steps pending: <d>`, and going on to the wiring step, which offers to write hooks into the project's settings. problem.after:
The review tool reads a code block inside a sprint's change body in two different ways, and the sprint form gives no rule for fencing such a body. So sprint certification fails a sprint whose change landed exactly as approved, and can count a change the sprint never wrote.

A sprint carries each change to the design corpus as a corpus delta: a heading such as `### New decision: <slug>`, then the artifact's whole new text, its body, inside a `` ```markdown `` fence. Sprint certification, `/converge sprint`, runs the review tool to compare each landed file with its body. [decision:final-form-deltas](.ok-planner/design/decisions/final-form-deltas.md) makes that comparison the test, and [story:certify-completion](.ok-planner/design/stories/certify-completion.md) promises that "done" means the same thing for every sprint. The [delta form](plugins/ok/families/ok-planner/skills/_shared/artifact-definitions.md#L277-L285) says nothing about a body that holds a code block.

To find delta headings, [review:fence_depths](plugins/ok/families/ok-planner/scripts/review#L1565-L1574) lets an info-string line such as `` ```sh `` open a nested fence and a bare backtick line close the innermost one. [review:inline_body](plugins/ok/families/ok-planner/scripts/review#L1607-L1614) cuts each body at the first later line equal to its opening fence. CommonMark, the reading Markdown renderers use, differs from both: inside an open fence an info-string line is text, and the first bare closer at least as long ends the outer fence.

A three-backtick body holding a bare code block, landed byte for byte, fails as "differs from the delta's body". Two fixes were sent back. Ending the body at its last closer dropped the next delta from the count. Reading by depth still let a bare inner block close the outer fence, so a heading-like line inside it added a phantom delta or dropped a real one. Four-backtick fences read correctly.

The ruling decides how a delta body may hold a code block, and what the tool does with a body that breaks that rule.

Sprint certification, `/converge sprint`, compares each landed file with its body, as [decision:final-form-deltas](.ok-planner/design/decisions/final-form-deltas.md) requires. [story:certify-completion](.ok-planner/design/stories/certify-completion.md) promises that "done" means the same for every sprint. The [delta form](plugins/ok/families/ok-planner/skills/_shared/artifact-definitions.md#L277-L285) says nothing about a body holding a code block.

recommendation.text:
The review tool reads fences in a sprint one way, CommonMark's, everywhere it reads them. The delta form says that a body holding code blocks uses a longer outer fence than any fence inside it. The tool refuses a body that breaks the rule, naming the delta and the rule, instead of guessing where the body ends.

problem.after:
Only true-up, the administration pass `/ok` runs, places the dashboard's page in a project, and git ignores the placed page. In every fresh clone or new worktree, the dashboard serves a stub that says to run `/ok`, and the owner must run a full true-up to see the page.

The dashboard is a local web page for working the issue intake. Each suite release carries one build of the page inside the installed front door, the `ok` plugin. [decision:pinned-build-placed-at-true-up](.ok-planner/design/decisions/pinned-build-placed-at-true-up.md) has true-up copy the build for the suite version the project is pinned to into the project, outside git, "never one retrieved when the owner opens the page." The [/dashboard skill](plugins/ok/families/ok-planner/skills/dashboard/SKILL.md) only starts the service and edits no file, per [decision:dashboard-started-by-skill](.ok-planner/design/decisions/dashboard-started-by-skill.md). The [service](plugins/ok/families/ok-planner/scripts/dashboard#L51) serves the stub when no page is placed. The [README](README.md#L30-L32) and the [integration contract](docs/integration-contract.md#L67-L69) promise that cloning a trued-up project "yields the working suite with nothing installed".

On 2026-10-22, in a project on ok-planner v28.0.0, `/dashboard` reported no page build. The owner did not want a true-up, which updates plugins and can rewrite the suite files copied into the project. Copying the installed 28.0.0 build into the project, as true-up does, made the page serve. The machine's plugin cache held four suite versions, so the pinned build is usually on disk. The owner asked that `/dashboard` place what it needs.

The ruling decides which act places the dashboard's page in a clone, or whether the clone promise narrows.

problem.after:
When `/ok` upgrades a project, it moves each old documentation declaration into the new docspec folder and leaves it in the old format. The docspec index then lists every moved file as declaring no location, so the lint and `/plan-docs` find no documentation behind any of them.

An earlier release declared each kind of documentation in a document type, a file under `.ok-planner/surface/documents/`. The current release declares it in a docspec, a file under `.ok-planner/docspec/` with different sections. True-up, the pass `/ok` runs to bring a project to the current layout, moves each document type to the docspec folder unchanged. The generated docspec index takes each location from the first line of a docspec's `## Where`, and writes "not declared" where that section is missing.

The administration document says a moved document type keeps its text until a sprint reshapes it. Three decisions rule that out. True-up leaves no earlier layout for the skills to meet ([decision:skills-read-only-the-current-layout](.ok-planner/design/decisions/skills-read-only-the-current-layout.md)). It may rewrite retired content in a docspec and nothing else ([decision:whole-file-ownership](.ok-planner/design/decisions/whole-file-ownership.md)). Outside a sprint, a docspec changes only through migrations that change no commitment ([decision:documentation-sprints-write-the-documentation](.ok-planner/design/decisions/documentation-sprints-write-the-documentation.md)). These leave one compliant end state: the docspec format, with the substance kept. The `target` front matter becomes `## Where`, `audience` becomes `## Reader`, `## Purpose` and `## Covers` merge into `## Covers`, and `## Notes` stays. The old format holds nothing for `## References` or `## Shape`, so those wait for a sprint. The one doubt is whether a docspec without them counts as the current layout.

In linescout-inl, a true-up to v28.0.0 on 2026-10-21 moved 17 document types unchanged. Every row of its docspec index reads "where: not declared; references: none".

problem.before:
True-up moves each document type an earlier release kept into the docspec folder with its text unchanged, so every moved file stays in the retired format. The owner then sees every docspec listed as "where: not declared", and `/plan-docs` finds no documentation behind any of them.

An earlier release declared each kind of documentation as a document type under `.ok-planner/surface/documents/`: front matter `document`, `audience`, and `target`, then `## Purpose`, `## Covers`, and `## Notes`. The current release declares it as a docspec under `.ok-planner/docspec/`: `docspec:` front matter, then `## Where`, `## Reader`, `## Covers`, `## References`, `## Shape`, and `## Notes`, among others. True-up, the pass `/ok` runs to bring a project's estate to the current layout, moves each document type and converts nothing. Its step message says "a document type is a docspec now". The generated docspec index reads the first line of each `## Where` and writes "not declared" where none stands, so the lint's doc-comment carve-out and `/plan-docs` read nothing either.

True-up brings the estate to the current layout "so the skills meet nothing an earlier layout left" ([decision:skills-read-only-the-current-layout](.ok-planner/design/decisions/skills-read-only-the-current-layout.md)). It may rewrite a retired key in a docspec and change nothing else ([decision:whole-file-ownership](.ok-planner/design/decisions/whole-file-ownership.md)), and a docspec changes outside a sprint only by "the administrator's migrations, which change no commitment" ([decision:documentation-sprints-write-the-documentation](.ok-planner/design/decisions/documentation-sprints-write-the-documentation.md)). These leave one compliant end state: the moved file in the docspec format, its substance kept. `target` becomes `## Where`, `audience` becomes `## Reader`, `## Purpose` with `## Covers` becomes `## Covers`, and `## Notes` stays. The old format holds no source for `## References` or `## Shape`, so those wait for a sprint; whether a docspec without them counts as the current layout is the one doubt in this reading. Filing one issue per file instead, as the filer also offered, leaves the retired format in place, which the first decision rules out.

In linescout-inl, a true-up to v28.0.0 on 2026-10-21 moved 17 document types unchanged, and every row of its docspec index reads "where: not declared; references: none".

problem.after:
/plan-tests takes no request to widen a story, and its planners never read which paths the earlier plan left out. A story an approved plan covered thinly stays thin.

/plan-tests plans a test sprint. Planner agents read each story and record scenarios, the outcomes a test must check. Each path a planner leaves out becomes a call, a choice the owner approves with the plan. The scenario list keeps no calls. The next run starts from the last test sprint's stamp and reads the files changed since. [Step 3](plugins/ok/families/ok-planner/skills/plan-tests/SKILL.md#L30) stops when nothing changed. When anything changed, [step 5](plugins/ok/families/ok-planner/skills/plan-tests/SKILL.md#L42) files a planner for every story. Each planner sorts its story's recorded scenarios and may add new ones, but reads none of the earlier calls. No step takes stories to widen.

On the linescout platform project, at ok-planner v28.0.0, on 2026-10-22, the first plan gave 13 stories one scenario and 13 stories two. 100 calls name a path left out, such as register-a-model's "One scenario, carried by gridiq formation apply; no control-route or console scenario". The owner wants those paths covered.

The ruling decides how /plan-tests revisits an approved plan to widen named stories.

[Step 2](plugins/ok/families/ok-planner/skills/plan-tests/SKILL.md#L24-L26) proposes `testing.run`, the command that runs one test, from how the project runs tests today. The tests tool [kills a test after 600 seconds](plugins/ok/families/ok-planner/scripts/tests#L106) unless the project declares another limit. `tests declare` [takes `--timeout`](plugins/ok/families/ok-planner/scripts/tests#L29), but step 2 never asks for one. Planners then choose how each test reaches the code, and no step after assembly asks whether the command can run each planned test in time. The first agent to meet a mismatch is a [test-writing task](plugins/ok/families/ok-planner/skills/plan-tests/core.md#L404-L405) inside the run. A test sprint runs under /goal and never stops to ask the owner, per [decision:test-loop-fixes-code-never-tests](.ok-planner/design/decisions/test-loop-fixes-code-never-tests.md), and its verifier sends back a fix that hides a failure behind [a longer timeout](plugins/ok/families/ok-planner/skills/plan-tests/core.md#L645). [decision:scenario-list-decided-once](.ok-planner/design/decisions/scenario-list-decided-once.md) commits the project to one run command.

On the linescout platform project, at ok-planner v28.0.0, on 2026-10-22, planners planned browser tests the declared command could not import, and long tests against a running stack that overran the 600-second limit. The test sprint stopped to ask about both. The owner said: "why are there questions for us? this should not be an interactive session. file any questions as issues".

The ruling decides when /plan-tests settles the runner and its time limit against the plan.

options.label: A
options.text: Check after assembly: /plan-tests compares each planned test's kind and setup with the runner and time limit, and asks the owner to change either before approval. Cost: one more question at approval, and a planner field naming each test's kind and setup.

recommendation.text:
/plan-tests asks the owner for the time limit when it proposes the command that runs one test, and every planner reads both. Each planned test names its kind and the setup it needs. After assembly, the session compares each planned test with the command and the limit, and asks the owner, before approval, to change either for any test they cannot run. The project keeps one run command. Rule this together with plan-tests-asks-the-owner-after-the-planners-run: both settle the owner's inputs before planning.

Rationale: option D moves every runner question into the interactive session, so the unattended run never needs the owner, as [decision:test-loop-fixes-code-never-tests](.ok-planner/design/decisions/test-loop-fixes-code-never-tests.md) requires. Planners that know the command plan tests it runs, and the check catches the rest where the owner can still answer. It keeps the one command [decision:scenario-list-decided-once](.ok-planner/design/decisions/scenario-list-decided-once.md) commits to, which option B would change. Option C leaves ways a story promises untested with no record. Option A alone leaves planners blind to the runner, so more tests reach the check. The flip case: if a project's tests need two runners that no single command can serve, even through a script that dispatches by path, option B's corpus change is the only way to test every way.

title: /plan-tests fixes the test runner before it knows what tests the plan needs

options.label: A
options.text: Qualify the row: retire applies to a scenario the stamp recorded, and a dropped way no scenario recorded gets no item. Cost: none beyond the prompt edit.

options.label: B
options.text: Accept retire on a first plan: the tool drops a retire item that names no recorded scenario, with a note. Cost: the tool silently absorbs a planner's mistake, which the project's coding rules forbid.

problem:
The /plan-tests story planner prompt tells a planner to retire a scenario its story dropped, and never says that retire applies only to a scenario an earlier plan recorded. On a first plan nothing is recorded, so each retire a planner files makes the plan's assembly fail, and the planner runs again.

/plan-tests plans a test sprint: one planner agent per story sorts each scenario, a way the story gives its benefit, into an action such as keep, new, or retire. The tests tool records the scenarios each approved plan holds, and its stamp marks the last test sprint. The [prompt's table](plugins/ok/families/ok-planner/skills/plan-tests/core.md#L123) reads: "The story's text dropped the scenario. | `retire`". The tool's assembly check, [tests:plan_failures](plugins/ok/families/ok-planner/scripts/tests#L619-L620), refuses a retire that names a scenario the stamp did not record. [decision:scenario-list-decided-once](.ok-planner/design/decisions/scenario-list-decided-once.md) has planners "sort every recorded scenario", so retire sorts a recorded scenario, and the tool already enforces that. [Step 7](plugins/ok/families/ok-planner/skills/plan-tests/SKILL.md#L58) answers a refusal by rerunning the planner whole.

On the linescout platform project, at ok-planner v28.0.0, on 2026-10-22, the first plan held 5 retire items from 4 planners. The task tracker has no verb to drop an item, so the owner approved editing the run file by hand to remove them.

The ruling decides how the prompt limits retire.

recommendation.text: The story planner prompt of /plan-tests limits retire to a scenario the stamp recorded. Its sorting table now reads "The story's text dropped the scenario. | retire". After, the row reads "The story's text dropped a scenario the stamp recorded. | retire", and the prompt adds that a way the story dropped which no scenario recorded gets no item. [decision:scenario-list-decided-once](.ok-planner/design/decisions/scenario-list-decided-once.md) forces the change: planners sort every recorded scenario, so retire is a sort of a recorded scenario, and the tests tool's assembly check already refuses any other. The prompt must name only items the decision and the tool accept. Nothing was applied.

options.label: A
options.text: Batch by shared code: one planner per group of stories whose code overlaps, up to a set size. Cost: a grouping pass reads the code before planning.

options.label: B
options.text: Batch by count: a fixed number of stories per planner, in catalog order. Cost: unrelated stories share an agent, so only the shared reads are saved.

options.label: C
options.text: Keep one planner per story. Cost: planning cost keeps growing with the story count.

options.label: D
options.text: Plan only what changed: after the first plan, plan only the stories that changed, whose tests failed, or whose cited code changed, and keep every other story's scenarios as recorded. Cost: no saving on a first plan, and a story whose uncited code changed is missed.

options.label: E
options.text: Batch by citation: group stories whose story annotations sit in the same files, up to a set size, and batch the rest by count. Cost: the grouping reaches only as far as the annotations do.

A planner sorts one story's scenarios, the ways the story gives its benefit. [Step 5](plugins/ok/families/ok-planner/skills/plan-tests/SKILL.md#L42) files "one story task per story". Any file changed since the last test sprint reopens planning, and every story is planned again.

On the linescout project, at ok-planner v28.0.0, on 2026-10-22, 107 stories got 107 story planners. They used 13.29 million of the 14.22 million planning tokens.

recommendation.text:
Group stories into planner tasks by the files that cite them, up to a set size, and batch uncited stories by count (E). A failure or a review finding on one story re-plans that story alone. After the first plan, plan only the stories a run's changes touch, counting a story whose recorded test failed in the planning run as touched, and keep every other story's scenarios as recorded (D). D changes what [decision:scenario-list-decided-once](.ok-planner/design/decisions/scenario-list-decided-once.md) says planners read.

Rationale: The linescout cost came from a first plan, which only batching cuts, and every later run with any change pays it again, which only D cuts. Citation grouping gets A's shared code reading from a search, where A pays for a code reading before planning and B saves only the shared reads. C keeps the growth. Re-planning one story alone keeps a refile from re-planning its whole batch. A widen run, if plan-tests-cannot-widen-an-approved-plan adds one, counts its named stories as touched. The flip case: if annotations cover few stories, E falls back to B nearly everywhere, and A's grouping pass earns its cost; if a later run misses a story whose uncited code changed, drop D and plan every story on each run.

messages.text: we have no opinion on this other than we want to reduce wasted time, tokens, and confusion. if an agent reading the boilerplate would expect cmd_prompt to be the source, then it should be. having a consistent interface will of course reduce friction

problem.after:
No command writes the sprint build prompt, so each session that runs a sprint copies an 8 KB fixed text and its shared rule blocks together by hand. That spends tokens on every sprint and leaves room for a copy that drops or alters a rule every build agent then follows.

The build prompt is the instructions every build agent of a sprint receives through the task tracker. It is the block {{SPRINT-BUILD-PROMPT}} in [.claude/skills/_sprint/shared.md](.claude/skills/_sprint/shared.md#L134), and it pulls in two other blocks, {{LEAF-AGENT-RULE}} and {{CONVERGE-CODING-RULES}}. Step 3 of every sprint's "How to execute this sprint" section, written from [plan-sprint/sprint-document.md](.claude/skills/plan-sprint/sprint-document.md#L106-L113), says to write that block "its transclusions resolved and `[SPRINT PATH]` filled". The review tool's `review prompt` command, [review:cmd_prompt](.ok-planner/bin/review#L529-L563), does this for /converge's prompts, but it reads templates only from `.claude/skills/converge/prompts/`, so `review prompt --name build` fails with "cannot read prompt template". [decision:single-source-transclusion](.ok-planner/design/decisions/single-source-transclusion.md) allows both paths: "The running model replaces each token when it assembles a dispatch; `/converge`'s review tool replaces them when it writes a run's prompts."

A template alone does not close the gap. `cmd_prompt` replaces a token only on a line of the template itself and pastes each block's text as written. It resolves no token inside a pasted block, and it fills no slot such as `[SPRINT PATH]` inside one; [the {{SPRINT-REVIEW-READING}} block](.claude/skills/_sprint/shared.md#L342) states that limit. {{SPRINT-BUILD-PROMPT}} is the one block that nests other blocks, and it carries `[SPRINT PATH]` in its own text. A template that names it would come out with {{LEAF-AGENT-RULE}}, {{CONVERGE-CODING-RULES}}, and `[SPRINT PATH]` left raw. Either option below therefore also needs `cmd_prompt` to resolve tokens and fill slots in pasted block text, recursively, and to drop the block's `Task prompt (profile ok-opus):` header line and its fence indent.

The archived build prompts in this project differ between sprints only in the sprint path and in suite updates between them. Sessions in this project and in the linescout-inl platform project have built the prompt with scratch scripts since 2026-10-17. A triage run retired an earlier filing of this gap as a defect claim, since nothing breaks today.

The owner ruled for the interface an agent reading the boilerplate expects: `review prompt`, called the way /converge calls it, writes the build prompt.

options.text: Fix review:hunt_settings so a `hunt.area_lines` that is not a positive whole number is refused with a message naming the key, and no wrong cut or crash follows.

problem:
The review tool reads `hunt.area_lines` from the review config without checking its value, so an operator who sets it to 0 or to text gets a wrong cut or a crash instead of a refusal that names the key.

`review areas` and `discover areas` cut the project's files into areas, each holding at most `hunt.area_lines` lines, read from `.ok-planner/review/config.json`. The function that reads the hunt settings refuses a missing key and checks `min`, `max`, and `lenses`, but takes `area_lines` as written. With a value of 0, every file overflows the budget, so each file becomes an area of its own. With a string, the size comparison raises a `TypeError` that reaches the owner frame as an internal error and never names the key.

A fixer saw this outside its brief during sprint certification of the sixth intake drain sprint; no merge agent judged it.

Site: [review:hunt_settings](plugins/ok/families/ok-planner/scripts/review#L637-L648), read by `review areas` and by [discover:cmd_areas](plugins/ok/families/ok-planner/scripts/discover#L165). Accept-list entry: A3 (an operator's input to a shipped script gives a wrong result or an error that does not say what they did wrong). Trigger: `hunt.area_lines` set to 0, a negative number, or a string. Evidence: `for key in ("min", "max", "threshold", "slice", "rotation", "area_lines", "lenses"): if key not in hunt: raise ReviewError(...)`, followed by assertions on `min`, `max`, and `lenses` alone; `chunked` cuts a new chunk when `chunk and weight + heft > budget`.
reason: No accept-list entry covers this defect claim. A string in hunt.area_lines raises in review:hunt_settings's callers and stops the program, which "What the list leaves standing" keeps (a grossly wrong value from the operator's own configuration where the program stops with an error); a 0 or negative value cuts each file into an area of its own, the nearest cut the value allows, which is no wrong result on a system configured correctly under A3.
title: The review tool checks that `hunt.area_lines` exists but not that it is a positive whole number

problem.after:
The tests tool starts one process per test, one test after another, and records a round's results only after the last test finishes. A project's suite therefore reruns its shared setup for every test, runs nothing in parallel, and loses every result when a round stops early.

A test sprint runs the project's tests in rounds through the tests tool's `run` verb. The tool reads `testing.run`, the project's command that runs one test. [`cmd_run`](plugins/ok/families/ok-planner/scripts/tests#L1398) calls [`run_one`](plugins/ok/families/ok-planner/scripts/tests#L1347) for each live test in turn ([line 1414](plugins/ok/families/ok-planner/scripts/tests#L1414)). `run_one` fills the test's `{path}` and `{name}` into the command through [`command_for`](plugins/ok/families/ok-planner/scripts/tests#L1340) and starts a new process. `cmd_run` [appends the round](plugins/ok/families/ok-planner/scripts/tests#L1415-L1423) to the sprint's `-results.jsonl` file only after every `run_one` returns. [decision:scenario-list-decided-once](.ok-planner/design/decisions/scenario-list-decided-once.md) commits to that shape: "The project declares how one test runs as `testing.run` in its configuration, a command holding `{path}` and, where the runner needs it, `{name}`."

On 2026-10-24, the first round of a test sprint on the linescout platform project ran 496 pytest tests this way. One measured test spent 20.85 s in setup and 0.71 s in its body. The project's session fixtures run once per pytest run, so one process per test reruns them for every test, and the suite would take roughly three hours. The owner stopped the round after 23 tests, and it recorded nothing.

The owner said: "ok-plugins should not own that loop. the test suite execution should belong to the project and the skill should deal with it generically". The owner's target is a full suite run in 10 minutes or less.

The ruling decides what the suite asks a project to declare so the project runs its own suite, and how the tests tool reads each test's result back into the round.

problem:
The tests tool runs a project's tests in one process per test, one after another, and records a round's results only after the last test ends. The owner decides what a project declares so the project runs its own suite, and how the tool reads each test's result back.

A test sprint runs the project's tests in rounds through the tests tool. The tool reads `testing.run`, the project's command that runs one test. problem.after:
The project's release boundary does not say whether a sprint approved but not yet started must keep working after the owner updates the suite with `/ok`. A test sprint approved on the last release cannot run after `/ok`.

problem.after:
The `/plan-docs` prompts check every claim of a docspec's documentation only when the docspec has no stamp, so a docspec whose stamp names a commit the repository no longer holds gets only its old claims rechecked. Its documentation can then ship claims no checker read, and the style pass fails when it runs `git diff` against the missing commit.

A docspec declares one kind of documentation a project keeps. Its stamp is the commit at which its documentation last passed a documentation sprint. Its claim ledger lists the claims that held then. [decision:docspec-stamp-opens-the-window](.ok-planner/design/decisions/docspec-stamp-opens-the-window.md) says "A docspec with no stamp, or with a stamp the repository no longer holds, is planned as new: its missing files are written whole, and every claim in its existing files is checked." [decision:documentation-claim-ledger](.ok-planner/design/decisions/documentation-claim-ledger.md) says a sprint checks every claim "in every file of a docspec planned as new".

A rebase can drop the stamp's commit. The `docs window` tool then reports the docspec as `new` and keeps its stamp in the entry. The planner, style, and checker prompts, the skill's window step, and the documentation sprint's fact-loop step all tie the full check to "no stamp". An agent that sees a stamp therefore checks only the ledger's claims.

An agent in one `/converge` run set a docspec's stamp to a missing commit. `docs window --json` printed `status: new` with the stamp set, and `git diff <stamp>` failed with `fatal: bad object`.

problem.after:
`/converge`'s drive prompt bans the git commands that undo an edit, even inside a scratch project, and names no other way to undo one. A driver, the agent that tries one story against the running product, then has no allowed way to put back a file it edited in scratch to probe the story.

[decision:drive-tries-each-story-as-a-user](.ok-planner/design/decisions/drive-tries-each-story-as-a-user.md) says a driver changes nothing in the project's tree: a command that may write runs against a scratch copy or a scratch project, never at the project root. The [drive prompt](plugins/ok/families/ok-planner/skills/converge/prompts/drive.md#L70) states that rule, then bans `git checkout`, `restore`, `reset`, `stash`, and `clean` with no scope. Six other `/converge` prompts carry the same ban for agents that read or edit the project root, where the ban protects uncommitted work. Only the driver writes in scratch, so only the driver meets the ban there.

On Oct 24, a driver ran `git checkout -- <file>` inside its scratch project to undo a probe edit. It touched nothing outside the scratch folder, which it then removed.

The ruling decides how a driver undoes an edit inside its own scratch project.

Keep the git ban whole in the drive prompt, and name the two ways a driver undoes a scratch edit: copy the file aside before a probe edit and copy it back afterward, or discard the scratch project and make a fresh one where a command wrote what no copy saved.

Rationale: Option C keeps one rule that reads the same way in all seven `/converge` prompts that carry it, and gives the driver an undo that cannot reach the project root. Option A asks a driver to judge whether its scratch copy shares a repository with the root. A wrong judgment rewrites the tree the run certifies, which [decision:drive-tries-each-story-as-a-user](.ok-planner/design/decisions/drive-tries-each-story-as-a-user.md) names as the reason drivers work in scratch. Option B alone makes every undo pay the full setup. Flip case: if drivers often need to undo writes that commands spread over many files, and a fresh scratch project costs minutes each time, option A pays, scoped to a repository the driver made with `git init` or a full copy.

problem.after:
`/plan-tests` keeps an old test's rule only where a project document states that rule, and otherwise deletes the test without asking. A test that enforces an unwritten layering or naming rule goes, and nothing checks that rule afterward.

A legacy suite is the tests a project had before it adopted the suite. A port rewrites a test as a check that runs on every review. The [sort prompt](plugins/ok/families/ok-planner/skills/plan-tests/core.md#L490-L506) reads the rules a test may enforce from the decisions, the practices, the release boundaries, and the rules files. [decision:legacy-suites-sorted-automatically](.ok-planner/design/decisions/legacy-suites-sorted-automatically.md) ports a test that "enforces a written rule on the code's shape", deletes one that checks "a behavior no story or rule names", and asks nothing per test. [story:retire-a-legacy-suite](.ok-planner/design/stories/retire-a-legacy-suite.md) promises the old suite does not leave "a rule it enforced unchecked".

A newly adopted project has few written rules, so most such tests go. The owner sees each deletion only as a line in the plan and the completion report's veto list.

The ruling decides whether the story covers every rule the old suite enforced, or only the written ones.

problem:
`/plan-sprint` drafts the changes the owner already decided before it updates the design record for work done outside any sprint, and no step merges the two drafts. Where both change one document, the sprint can carry two full copies of it, and the later copy drops the change the earlier one made.

The design corpus is that record of what the product commits to. A sprint changes a corpus document through a delta, which holds the document's whole new text. Execution copies that text into place.

Frame, the second phase of `/plan-sprint`, drafts each ruled issue, one the owner already decided, "in final form". Reconcile, the third phase, then walks each change made outside any sprint with the owner, and its "Corpus catches up" outcome drafts deltas that bring the affected documents in line with that work.

Reconcile's text says it runs "before anything is drafted on top of it", but Frame has already drafted. The later Resolve phase tells the agent to amend the draft where an answer "collides with a delta already drafted". No sentence says the same for a Reconcile outcome.

An agent of a `/converge` run read the phases in order and found no step that rebuilds a Frame delta on a Reconcile outcome. A merge agent confirmed the defect.

problem.after:
This project's `/converge` settings give no command to stop what a driver starts, so `/converge` cannot clean up after a driver that quits early. Each run it leaves open stays in the stack tool's registry, with its temp folder, until someone removes it by hand.

In a drive, `/converge` hands each story to a driver: an agent that tries the story against the product as a user would. A driver that needs a scratch project opens a run with the project's stack tool, `stack up`, under a drive name `/converge` gives it, and closes it with `stack down` when done. The review facts, `.ok-planner/review/project.md`, give these commands. After the drivers finish, `/converge` files one stop task per drive name, with the command `review drive-command --role resource-stop` prints, so a run a driver left open still closes.

The review facts' `## Drive commands` section declares no stack and gives no `resource-stop` line. The command refuses, every stop task fails, and `/converge` goes on. [decision:run-artifacts-removed-with-the-run](.ok-planner/design/decisions/run-artifacts-removed-with-the-run.md) commits that "A run's artifacts end with the run", pass or fail, and [story:verification-leaves-no-artifacts-behind](.ok-planner/design/stories/verification-leaves-no-artifacts-behind.md) promises each verification run's artifacts removed once the run is over.

problem.after:
A sprint's close step tells the session to stop when the completion check fails, before it asks the owner which calls to veto. The owner sees the certification's calls in the report but is never asked to veto one, and a later certification run renders only its own calls.

A call is a judgment an agent made without the owner. Each sprint ends with fixed execution steps, written from the sprint document template. Step 13 renders the completion report and runs `review certified`, the completion check, which prints `SPRINT COMPLETE` or `SPRINT NOT COMPLETE`. It then presents the report's calls table and asks which rows the owner vetoes. On `SPRINT NOT COMPLETE`, step 13 says "stop" and only after that "Then present", so a session that follows it ends the close with no veto question. The test sprint and documentation sprint templates instead work each failure their check names.

[decision:converge-close-takes-vetoes](.ok-planner/design/decisions/converge-close-takes-vetoes.md) commits that "Every `/converge` run closes the same way, whatever its mode", that its close asks which rows the owner vetoes, and that "In sprint certification, the sprint's execution steps make this close". It rejects leaving the owner to file an issue by hand. [story:veto-calls-made-in-my-absence](.ok-planner/design/stories/veto-calls-made-in-my-absence.md) promises a way to overturn each call.

The [script returns](plugins/ok/families/ok-planner/skills/_tasks/drain.md#L22) only when the run is done, waiting, stuck, paused, or failed, and first waits for every agent in flight.

[decision:drain-runs-as-a-workflow-script](.ok-planner/design/decisions/drain-runs-as-a-workflow-script.md) says "The session wakes once per drain", because each wake rereads the session's whole context. problem.after:
No suite text tells a test sprint's agents how a test waits for the product, so they write tests that sleep and poll on elapsed time. The owner chooses whether to restore the retired testing standard, which agents it binds, and what enforces it.

A test sprint is the one run that writes tests. Its test tasks write each test, and a loop then runs the suite, fixes the code for each failing test, and has a verifier read each fix. Release v22.0.0, on 2026-09-12, deleted the suite's testing standard and the coding rule that restated it. The standard said a test's verdict never depends on elapsed time. A test waits on events the product emits, never on a sleep, a deadline poll, or a timeout. The product takes its clock and timers from outside, so a test can drive them.

The test sprint came later and carries none of this. The [test-writing prompt](plugins/ok/families/ok-planner/skills/plan-tests/core.md#L764) says nothing about waits. The [fix prompt](plugins/ok/families/ok-planner/skills/plan-tests/core.md#L973) and the [verify prompt](plugins/ok/families/ok-planner/skills/plan-tests/core.md#L1041) refuse only a fix that adds a longer timeout or a retry. The verifier reads fixes alone, as [decision:test-loop-fixes-code-never-tests](.ok-planner/design/decisions/test-loop-fixes-code-never-tests.md) sets, so a test written to sleep passes. The per-test limit, [`testing.timeout`](plugins/ok/families/ok-planner/skills/plan-tests/SKILL.md#L28-L32), caps one test and forbids no sleep.

On the linescout project, at ok-planner v28.0.0, the first test sprint (2026-10-22) wrote 496 tests. They held 223 `sleep` calls, 187 of them inside polling loops, and 417 deadline reads. One serial round took about 3.7 hours, mostly between identical polls and on product timers the tests could not drive. The owner restored the standard there as a project rule.

The ruling decides where the wait rules live, which agents they bind, and whether a reader or a check enforces them.

title.after: Whether the suite restores its testing standard, and what enforces it
title.before: Restore the testing standard so tests wait on events, not elapsed time

messages.text: Title names the decision; context reordered and trimmed.

Restore the testing standard as a suite standards document, carry its condensed rules in the cheatsheet's Tests section, cite it from the test-writing, fix, and verify prompts, and widen the verifier to read each written test as well as each fix, sending back any test or fix whose verdict waits on elapsed time.

Rationale: the suite already keeps its events and writing standards this way, as a full document with an ambient copy in the cheatsheet every agent loads. The wait rules bind product code as much as tests: the product must take its clock from outside and emit the events a test waits on. Only the cheatsheet reaches the build agents that write that code, which B misses. C makes completion depend on elapsed time, the dependence the standard forbids in a verdict, and ties a pass to the machine. D adds patterns per language where a reader already covers the case. Flip case: if a test sprint run under the restored standard and the widened verifier still ships tests that sleep or poll, a reader is not enough, and D's check earns its false hits under the cheatsheet's rule that every written constraint needs a check that fails on violation.

options.label: A
options.text: Restore the testing standard as a suite document beside the events and writing standards, condense it into the cheatsheet's Tests section, cite it from the test-writing, fix, and verify prompts, and have the verifier read each written test as well as each fix, sending back any that sleeps or polls on elapsed time. Cost: one more standards document, and a change to [decision:test-loop-fixes-code-never-tests](.ok-planner/design/decisions/test-loop-fixes-code-never-tests.md) so the verifier reads tests.

options.label: B
options.text: Write the rules into the test-writing, fix, and verify prompts alone, with no standards document. Cost: the rules that bind product code, an injected clock and progress events a test can wait on, reach no build agent, so a test sprint still meets timers no test can drive.

options.label: C
options.text: Do A, and add a round budget beside [`testing.timeout`](plugins/ok/families/ok-planner/skills/plan-tests/SKILL.md#L28-L32), with `tests complete` refusing a round over budget. Cost: completion then depends on the speed of the machine the round ran on.

options.label: D
options.text: Do A, and add a mechanical check that scans each written test for sleeps and deadline reads and fails its test task. Cost: patterns per language, and false hits on sleeps against a fake clock.

problem.after:
The lint asks git for a file's committed copy by a path relative to the project root, but git reads that path from the top of the repository. Where the project root is a repository's subfolder, the lookup always fails. The lint then reports a marker an earlier release committed as new, and blocks every edit to that file.

The lint is the suite's comment checker, and an edit hook runs it on each file an agent edits. A file that carried the `@plumbline:allow-docstrings` marker in an earlier release keeps its doc comments while the marker stays committed. The lint refuses a marker an edit adds, so it runs `git show HEAD:<path>` and checks the committed copy for the marker. Git reads a path after `HEAD:` from the repository's top folder, unless the path starts with `./` or `../`. The suite finds the project root by its estate folder, never by `.git`, so the suite works in a repository's subfolder, as [decision:filesystem-discovery-markers](.ok-planner/design/decisions/filesystem-discovery-markers.md) says. The lint's own changed-file check already resolves git's paths against the repository's top folder, in [plumbline:changedPaths](plugins/ok/families/ok-planner/scripts/plumbline#L1432-L1455), and the review tool already passes `HEAD:./<path>` in [review](plugins/ok/families/ok-planner/scripts/review#L1395).

In a project at a repository's `platform/` folder, the edit hook blocked edits to two files whose markers an earlier release committed, at `src/gridiq/simsdk/transport.py:5` and `src/gridiq/simsdk/source.py:3`, saying a new marker is refused.

Site: [plumbline:committedLegacyMarker](plugins/ok/families/ok-planner/scripts/plumbline#L594-L598). Entry: A9, the system reports something false that someone acts on: the lint's message and exit code tell the agent its marker is new when it is committed, and the edit hook blocks the edit. Trigger: lint any file that carries a committed marker, in a project whose root is not the repository's top folder. Evidence, [plumbline:596](plugins/ok/families/ok-planner/scripts/plumbline#L596): `const shown = spawnSync('git', ['show', `HEAD:${rel}`], { cwd: config.repoRoot, encoding: 'utf8' });`, where `rel` comes from `path.relative(config.repoRoot, filePath)` at [plumbline:585](plugins/ok/families/ok-planner/scripts/plumbline#L585).

The lint's own changed-file check already resolves git's paths against the repository's top folder, in [plumbline:changedPaths](plugins/ok/families/ok-planner/scripts/plumbline#L1432-L1455), and the review tool already passes `HEAD:./<path>` in [review](plugins/ok/families/ok-planner/scripts/review#L1395).

In a project at a repository's `platform/` folder, the edit hook blocked edits to two files whose markers an earlier release committed, at `src/gridiq/simsdk/transport.py:5` and `src/gridiq/simsdk/source.py:3`, saying a new marker is refused.

Site: [plumbline:committedLegacyMarker](plugins/ok/families/ok-planner/scripts/plumbline#L594-L598). Entry: A9, the system reports something false that someone acts on: the lint's message and exit code tell the agent its marker is new when it is committed, and the edit hook blocks the edit. Trigger: lint any file that carries a committed marker, in a project whose root is not the repository's top folder. Evidence, [plumbline:596](plugins/ok/families/ok-planner/scripts/plumbline#L596): `const shown = spawnSync('git', ['show', `HEAD:${rel}`], { cwd: config.repoRoot, encoding: 'utf8' });`, where `rel` comes from `path.relative(config.repoRoot, filePath)` at [plumbline:585](plugins/ok/families/ok-planner/scripts/plumbline#L585).

recommendation.text: Fix [plugins/ok/families/ok-planner/scripts/plumbline:committedLegacyMarker](plugins/ok/families/ok-planner/scripts/plumbline#L594-L598) so a marker committed in a project whose root is a subfolder of its repository is no longer reported as a new marker.

title: The lint looks up committed files by a path git reads from the wrong folder
